Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
• Category: Resectable upfront  
• Reasoning:  
  – Imaging (CT and MRI) shows only two liver metastases, each ≤3.5 cm, located in segments V and VIII, allowing a right‑anterior sectorectomy or two non‑anatomic wedge resections with an anticipated future liver remnant > 30 % (technical criteria satisfied).

Woman, 70 years old, operated for low rectal cancer 3 years ago (T3N1M0) after chemoradiotherapy. CEA 95 ng/mL. Liver MRI: lesion in segment II (2.5 cm) and micronodule segment V. RAS wild-type, MSS.
MDT Discussion: Metachronous metastases, potentially curable, negative extra-hepatic workup.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront  

Reasoning: The patient has only two liver lesions – a 2.5 cm metastasis in segment II and a sub‑centimetre micronodule in segment V. Both are amenable to limited, non‑anatomic or segmental resections that will leave a future liver remnant well above the 30 % (or >0.5 % body‑weight) threshold. The lesions are not adjacent to major hepatic veins, the portal/hepatic arterial inflow and outflow can be preserved, and there is no extra‑hepatic disease on staging. Thus, from both technical and oncologic standpoints the disease meets criteria for immediate curative‑intent surgery without a prerequisite systemic‑therapy interval.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  

1. Pre‑operative work‑up  
   • Full liver function panel, indocyanine‑green clearance or 99mTc‑mebrofenin scan if any concern for underlying steatosis or cholestasis.  
   • Volumetric CT or MRI to confirm future liver remnant ≥ 30 % (or FLR/BW > 0.5 %).  
   • Repeat high‑resolution liver MRI (including hepatobiliary phase) to verify that no additional occult lesions are present.  
   • Baseline performance status (ECOG 0‑1) and cardiopulmonary assessment given age 70.  

2. Surgical plan – Upfront liver‑first approach  
   • Laparoscopic (or open if anatomy dictates) left lateral segmentectomy (segment II) plus a non‑anatomic wedge resection of the segment V micronodule.  
   • Intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion locations and exclude additional disease.  
   • Aim for R0 margins (≥ 1 mm) while preserving at least two contiguous segments; expected FLR ≈ 70 % after resection.  

3. Post‑operative systemic therapy – Adjuvant (or peri‑operative) chemotherapy  
   • Given the markedly elevated CEA (95 ng/mL) – a high‑risk biological marker – and RAS‑wild‑type status, recommend 6 months of FOLFOX (5‑FU/leucovorin/oxaliplatin) with addition of an anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab) as adjuvant treatment.  
   • If postoperative recovery is delayed or liver function is borderline, the regimen can be started 6‑8 weeks after surgery.  

4. Surveillance  
   • CEA measurement and contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (or CT) every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months up to 5 years.  
   • Colonoscopic surveillance per standard rectal‑cancer follow‑up (typically at 1 year, then every 2‑3 years).  

Step 3 – Missing data  

 Current liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin, ICG clearance).  
 Quantitative future liver remnant volume (or FLR/BW ratio).  
 Performance status / comorbidity profile (cardiovascular, pulmonary, renal).  
 Exact size and radiologic characteristics of the segment V micronodule.  
 Details of any residual rectal disease or symptoms that might require concurrent colorectal surgery.  

These items are needed to confirm surgical fitness and to fine‑tune the peri‑operative chemotherapy plan, but the available information already supports a recommendation for upfront curative liver resection.

Case_Content:
Man, 68 years old, history of left colectomy for T4N2 tumor, in remission for 2 years. Surveillance: CEA 430 ng/mL. FDG-PET: three bilobar liver lesions, 2-3 cm, no other foci. BRAF wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Metachronous liver recurrence, potentially resectable after discussion.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Category: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning:  
- Three bilobar metastases each 2‑3 cm are within the size and number limits that can be removed while preserving a future liver remnant (FLR) ≥30 % in most patients.  
- No extra‑hepatic disease is identified on PET, and the primary tumour has already been resected, satisfying the oncologic criteria for a curative intent approach.  
- Critical information required to confirm technical feasibility is missing: quantitative volumetric imaging to calculate the FLR, liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, platelet count), and the patient’s performance status/comorbidities. Without these data we cannot guarantee that a safe R0 resection leaving adequate liver reserve is possible. Hence the case is classified as “Potentially resectable” pending completion of these assessments.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Pre‑operative systemic therapy  
   - Initiate a peri‑operative chemotherapy regimen (e.g., 6 cycles of FOLFOX or FOLFIRI combined with a biologic agent such as bevacizumab or anti‑EGFR therapy, guided by KRAS status when available).  
   - Objectives: (a) treat micrometastatic disease, (b) obtain a “test of time” to confirm disease biology (stable or responding disease), (c) potentially downsize lesions to facilitate a less extensive hepatectomy.  

2. Restaging after chemotherapy  
   - Perform high‑resolution contrast‑enhanced MRI of the liver (or CT with liver protocol) with volumetric analysis to:  
      Re‑assess number, size, and anatomical relationship of each lesion.  
      Calculate FLR; if FLR <30 % (or <0.5 % liver‑body weight ratio) consider portal vein embolisation (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy.  
   - Repeat CEA and PET‑CT to confirm absence of new extra‑hepatic disease.  

3. Surgical planning  
   - If FLR is adequate after restaging: proceed to a single‑stage, margin‑negative (R0) liver resection.  
      Preferred approach: anatomical or parenchymal‑sparing resections of the involved segments (e.g., left lateral sectionectomy plus non‑anatomic resection of right‑lobe lesions) to preserve maximal liver parenchyma.  
   - If FLR is insufficient:  
      Perform PVE of the liver lobe bearing the larger tumor burden, re‑image after 2–4 weeks to document hypertrophy, then complete resection in a second operation.  
      Alternatively, consider a two‑stage hepatectomy with clearance of the less‑affected lobe first, followed by PVE and delayed resection of the diseased lobe.  
   - Intra‑operative ultrasound to detect any occult lesions and to refine resection margins.  

4. Post‑operative management  
   - Resume/adapt systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 3–6 cycles of the same regimen) as adjuvant therapy, unless contraindicated by postoperative recovery.  
   - Serial CEA monitoring and imaging (CT/MRI) every 3–6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  

5. Multidisciplinary follow‑up  
   - Ongoing review by the MDT (surgical, medical oncology, radiology, pathology) to adjust therapy based on pathological response, margin status, and postoperative liver function.

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Current performance status (ECOG/ASA) and detailed comorbidity profile.  
- Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, AST/ALT, INR, platelet count).  
- Quantitative volumetric imaging to calculate future liver remnant (CT or MRI with liver‑specific contrast).  
- Precise anatomical location of each metastasis relative to major vessels/ducts.  
- KRAS mutation status (to guide choice of biologic agent).  
- Details of any prior adjuvant chemotherapy received after the original left colectomy.  

These data are essential to finalize resectability, select the optimal systemic regimen, and plan the surgical sequence safely.

Case_Content:
Man, 67 years old, left colectomy for T4N2M0 colon cancer 18 months ago. Surveillance: CEA 380 ng/mL. Liver MRI: four bilobar lesions, 2 to 3.5 cm.thoracic CT scan negative for metastases. BRAF wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Metachronous liver recurrence, potentially resectable based on volumetric assessment.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
- Four bilobar metastases (2‑3.5 cm) are technically amenable to R0 resection, but the MDT report cites “potentially resectable based on volumetric assessment,” indicating that the future liver remnant (FLR) is borderline.  
- A prerequisite intervention (FLR augmentation such as portal vein embolisation, or a trial of neoadjuvant chemotherapy to confirm favourable tumour biology) is required before a definitive curative‑intent hepatectomy can be performed.  
- No extra‑hepatic disease is identified and the patient is BRAF‑wild type, which supports a curative intent, but the missing quantitative FLR data precludes classifying the case as “Resectable upfront.”  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Induction systemic therapy  
  • Start a modern doublet (e.g., FOLFOX or FOLFIRI) combined with a biologic agent (anti‑VEGF or anti‑EGFR, guided by RAS status when available).  
  • Aim for 2–3 months of treatment to (a) assess disease biology (“test of time”) and (b) potentially downsize lesions.  
  • Re‑measure CEA after each cycle; a falling trend supports proceeding to surgery.  

- Re‑assessment of liver volume  
  • Perform repeat liver MRI with volumetry (or CT‑based volumetry) after induction therapy.  
  • If FLR ≥ 30 % of total liver volume (or >0.5 % body weight) – proceed to surgery.  
  • If FLR remains insufficient, schedule right‑portal vein embolisation (PVE) to induce hypertrophy; re‑image 3–4 weeks later.  

- Surgical plan  
  • If FLR adequate after induction – consider a single‑stage, parenchyma‑sparing hepatectomy (e.g., left lateral sectionectomy + limited right‑lobe resections) aiming for negative margins (R0) while preserving ≥30 % FLR.  
  • If FLR inadequate – adopt a two‑stage approach:  
    – Stage 1: Resection of left‑lateral lesions + right‑portal vein embolisation.  
    – Stage 2 (4–6 weeks later): Right hepatectomy (or extended right resection) once FLR has hypertrophied to ≥30 %.  
  • Intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion location and achieve clear margins; consider adjunctive thermal ablation for lesions in difficult locations.  

- Post‑operative management  
  • Resume/adapt systemic therapy (e.g., 3–6 months of adjuvant FOLFOX ± biologic) based on pathology and postoperative recovery.  
  • Serial CEA monitoring and imaging (CT/MRI) every 3–6 months for the first two years, then annually.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Performance status (ECOG/ASA) and detailed comorbidity profile.  
- Baseline liver function tests and quantitative FLR volume or FLR/body‑weight ratio.  
- RAS mutation status (KRAS/NRAS) and MSI/MMR status to guide biologic choice.  
- Details of prior adjuvant therapy after the primary resection (agents, duration).  
- Exact anatomical relationship of each metastasis to major vessels/ducts (to plan parenchyma‑sparing vs. major resection).  
- Patient’s cardiopulmonary reserve (e.g., VO₂ max) to confirm fitness for major hepatic surgery.
Reference:

The patient presents with four metachronous bilobar liver metastases (2–3.5 cm) without evidence of extrahepatic disease. Although distributed in both lobes, the limited number and size of lesions suggest that parenchymal-sparing resections could achieve R0 margins while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited bilobar metachronous metastases, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging and volumetric assessment
• Perform high-resolution contrast-enhanced CT to precisely define the segmental distribution and vascular/biliary relationships of the 4 lesions.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR) to confirm feasibility of a single-stage approach.

B. Consider short peri-operative systemic therapy
• Given the high CEA level (380 ng/mL) and early recurrence (18 months), a short course (2–3 months) of peri-operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) is advisable to treat micrometastatic disease and assess tumor biology.
• BRAF wild-type does not modify the surgical indication.

C. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT-scan after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and reassess lesion relationships.

D. Surgical management after restaging
• If resectability and adequate FLR are confirmed, perform parenchymal-sparing resections or ablation of the four lesions guided by intra-operative ultrasound aiming for R0 margins.
• Depending on lesion distribution and FLR, this may be performed in a single stage or staged approach.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging at 3-month intervals.

B. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
C. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
E. Details of any adjuvant chemotherapy received after the initial colectomy.
G. Exact CEA trend over time prior to detection of the lesion.

Case_Content:
Woman, 54 years old, right colon adenocarcinoma resected 3 years earlier. CEA 520 ng/mL. at the abdominal CT scan: two liver metastases (segments II and VI), sizes 3.1 and 4.0 cm. KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Bilobar metachronous liver recurrence, anatomically possible.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Category: Resectable upfront  
Reasoning:  
- Imaging shows only two lesions (3.1 cm in segment II and 4.0 cm in segment VI) that are amenable to non‑anatomic wedge resections while preserving at least two contiguous liver segments.  
- No extra‑hepatic disease is reported; the disease is metachronous (3 years after primary resection), which favors a favorable biology for surgery.  
- Technical criteria for an adequate future liver remnant (FLR > 30 % in a non‑cirrhotic liver) are likely met given the limited tumor burden, although volumetry has not been provided.  
- KRAS mutation and a markedly elevated CEA (520 ng/mL) are adverse prognostic factors but do not preclude resection; they influence the systemic‑therapy strategy rather than technical feasibility.  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Baseline systemic assessment  
   - Obtain chest CT (or PET‑CT) to exclude occult pulmonary or other extra‑hepatic metastases.  
   - Perform liver volumetry (CT‑based or MRI) to confirm FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 40 % if prior chemotherapy is given).  
   - Review performance status (ECOG 0‑1), liver function tests, and comorbidities.  

2. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (proof‑of‑time)  
   - Initiate 3–4 months of oxaliplatin‑based doublet chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX or CAPEOX) combined with bevacizumab (anti‑VEGF), given KRAS mutation excludes anti‑EGFR agents.  
   - Rationale: high CEA and KRAS mutation confer a high clinical‑risk score; pre‑operative chemotherapy provides disease‑control, assesses tumor biology, and may improve R0 resection rates.  

3. Restaging after chemotherapy  
   - Repeat triphasic liver CT or liver‑specific MRI to evaluate tumor response and re‑measure FLR.  
   - If both lesions remain resectable with adequate FLR and no new lesions appear, proceed to surgery.  

4. Surgical plan  
   - Perform a single‑stage, parenchyma‑sparing hepatectomy: non‑anatomic wedge resection of segment II lesion and segment VI lesion, aiming for R0 margins (≥ 1 mm).  
   - Intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion location and exclude additional occult metastases.  
   - If FLR is borderline (<30 % after resection), consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage approach (resection of the smaller lesion first, followed by hypertrophy‑inducing PVE and delayed resection of the second lesion).  

5. Post‑operative management  
   - Resume adjuvant chemotherapy to complete a total of 6 months of systemic therapy (including the neoadjuvant course).  
   - Serial CEA monitoring (every 3 months) and imaging surveillance (contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of the liver every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually).  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Quantitative liver function and volumetry to confirm adequate FLR.  
- Comprehensive staging for extra‑hepatic disease (chest imaging, possibly PET‑CT).  
- Patient’s performance status, comorbidities, and baseline laboratory values (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelets).  
- Details of any prior systemic therapy received after the primary resection.  
- Information on the original primary tumor pathology (T‑stage, N‑stage, margin status) to refine prognostic assessment.

Case_Content:
Man, 60 years old, right colectomy for T3N1 tumor 2 years ago. CEA 140 ng/mL. Liver MRI: three liver metastases (IV, V, VI), sizes 2 to 3 cm. RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Limited liver involvement, no other locations.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
- Classification: Resectable upfront  
- Reasoning:  
  • Three metastases (2‑3 cm) are confined to segments IV, V and VI, allowing a parenchyma‑sparing resection (segmentectomy or limited anatomical resection) while preserving at least two contiguous liver segments (I‑II‑III‑VII‑VIII).  
  • No radiological evidence of extra‑hepatic disease; liver‑only disease.  
  • RAS wild‑type and no prior hepatotoxic chemotherapy reported, suggesting normal liver parenchyma and adequate functional reserve.  
  • Technical criteria for resectability (R0 resection possible, preservation of inflow/outflow, biliary drainage, and anticipated future liver remnant > 30 % in a healthy liver) are met.  
  • High CEA (140 ng/mL) is an adverse prognostic marker but does not preclude surgery; it supports the use of peri‑operative systemic therapy but does not make resection contingent on down‑staging.  

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Pre‑operative work‑up:  
  • Full liver function panel, coagulation profile, indocyanine‑green clearance (if available) to confirm hepatic reserve.  
  • Volumetric CT or MRI to calculate future liver remnant (FLR); target ≥ 30 % for a healthy liver.  
  • Chest CT (or PET‑CT) to reconfirm absence of extra‑hepatic disease.  
  • Assessment of performance status (ECOG 0‑1) and comorbidities.  
- Surgical plan:  
  • Perform a parenchyma‑sparing resection of segments IV, V and VI (either three separate segmentectomies or a combined limited right anterior hepatectomy) aiming for R0 margins (≥ 1 mm).  
  • Intra‑operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and exclude occult disease.  
  • Preserve at least two contiguous segments with intact inflow/outflow and biliary drainage.  
- Peri‑operative systemic therapy:  
  • Administer peri‑operative (neoadjuvant) chemotherapy is optional; given the disease is technically resectable, the preferred approach is upfront surgery followed by adjuvant chemotherapy.  
  • Recommended adjuvant regimen: 6 months of FOLFOX (or CAPOX) plus an anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab) because the tumor is RAS wild‑type and the CEA is markedly elevated, indicating higher risk of micrometastatic disease.  
  • If the patient had received extensive prior chemotherapy with signs of liver injury, consider a short course of pre‑operative chemotherapy (2–3 cycles) to assess tumor biology, but this is not mandatory here.  
- Post‑operative follow‑up:  
  • CEA measurement and contrast‑enhanced MRI or CT of the liver every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months up to 5 years.  
  • Surveillance of the colon anastomosis site with colonoscopy at 1 year and then per guidelines.

- Liver function and synthetic capacity (bilirubin, albumin, INR, ICG clearance).  
- Volumetric assessment of the future liver remnant.  
- Detailed performance status (ECOG/ASA) and comorbidity profile (cardiovascular, pulmonary, diabetes, etc.).  
- Prior systemic therapy exposure and any chemotherapy‑associated liver injury (steatosis, sinusoidal obstruction).  
- Full thoracic imaging (CT or PET‑CT) to definitively exclude pulmonary or other extra‑hepatic metastases.  
- Baseline renal function and hematologic parameters to confirm suitability for adjuvant chemotherapy.

Case_Content:
Woman, 74 years old, rectal cancer resected 5 years ago, new CEA elevation to 600 ng/mL. at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan: single liver metastasis segment IVa (4.2 cm). KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Late solitary metastasis, potentially curable situation.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
 The solitary 4.2 cm lesion in segment IVa is technically amenable to an anatomic segment IVa/IVb resection or an extended left hepatectomy, provided that a future liver remnant (FLR) of ≥30 % of total liver volume (or ≥0.5 % of body weight) can be preserved.  
 No extra‑hepatic disease is reported, but the case lacks essential data that directly determines surgical feasibility (FLR volumetry, liver function, performance status, comorbidities). Because this information is missing, the lesion cannot be declared “Resectable upfront.”  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
 Step 2.1 – Complete staging  
  - Perform high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast (or contrast‑enhanced CT if MRI unavailable) to confirm solitary disease and to delineate vascular anatomy.  
  - Obtain chest CT (or PET‑CT) to exclude pulmonary or other extra‑hepatic metastases.  
  - Calculate FLR volume using CT‑based volumetry; assess liver function (ICG clearance, bilirubin, albumin, platelet count) and cardiopulmonary fitness (ASA, ECOG).  

 Step 2.2 – Biological “test of time”  
  - Given the markedly elevated CEA (600 ng/mL) and KRAS mutation (negative prognostic marker), initiate a short course (2–3 months) of modern doublet chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) to assess disease biology and obtain a biochemical response.  
  - Re‑measure CEA after chemotherapy; a ≥50 % decline would support proceeding to surgery, whereas progression would prompt continuation of systemic therapy or alternative local therapies.  

 Step 2.3 – Surgical plan (contingent on Step 2.1 results)  
  - If FLR ≥30 % and liver function acceptable, proceed with curative‑intent hepatic resection: an anatomic segment IVa/IVb resection with negative (R0) margins, preserving at least two contiguous segments and adequate inflow/outflow.  
  - Intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm absence of occult lesions and to guide precise transection.  
  - If FLR is insufficient, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) to hypertrophy the contralateral liver, followed by delayed resection.  

 Step 2.4 – Adjuvant therapy  
  - After R0 resection and recovery, resume systemic chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) for 3–6 months as adjuvant treatment, given high‑risk features (age > 70, KRAS‑mutated, high pre‑operative CEA).  

 Step 2.5 – Surveillance  
  - Serial CEA every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months; imaging (CT or MRI) at 6‑month intervals for the first 2 years, then annually.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
 Quantitative FLR volume (or liver‑to‑body‑weight ratio).  
 Detailed liver function tests (bilirubin, albumin, ICG clearance, platelet count).  
 Patient’s performance status (ECOG/ASA) and comorbidity profile (cardiovascular, pulmonary, renal).  
 Confirmation of absence of extra‑hepatic disease (chest CT or PET‑CT).  
 Precise vascular anatomy of the lesion (relationship to middle hepatic vein, portal pedicle) to determine whether a limited segmentectomy is feasible or an extended left hepatectomy is required.

Woman, 68 years old, T3N2 rectal tumor operated 4 years ago. CEA 78 ng/mL. Liver MRI: two metastases segments III and VI (2 and 2.6 cm), no extra-hepatic involvement.
MDT Discussion: Bilobar metachronous recurrence, anatomically simple.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront  
- Two liver metastases, each ≤3 cm, located in segments III and VI, are amenable to non‑anatomic wedge resection or limited segmentectomy.  
- Bilobar distribution does not preclude resection because the remaining liver volume after removing segments III and VI exceeds the commonly accepted ≥30 % future liver remnant (FLR) threshold.  
- No extra‑hepatic disease is identified on imaging.  
- The primary rectal cancer was resected 4 years ago and is currently disease‑free.  
- Although the CEA is elevated (78 ng/mL), it is below the >200 ng/mL level that is often considered a relative contraindication.  
- All technical and oncologic criteria for curative‑intent hepatectomy are satisfied; therefore surgery can be offered immediately.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Confirm baseline status  
   - Perform a contrast‑enhanced CT of chest and abdomen (or PET‑CT) and a colonoscopic examination to exclude occult recurrence.  
   - Obtain tumor molecular profile (RAS, BRAF, MSI/dMMR) and baseline liver function tests, ECOG/ASA status.  

2. Neoadjuvant systemic therapy (optional but advisable)  
   - Because CEA is markedly elevated and to obtain “proof of time,” give 3–4 cycles of a doublet regimen (FOLFOX or CAPOX) ± bevacizumab, tailored to molecular results.  
   - Re‑image the liver with MRI after chemotherapy to verify disease stability or response and to reconfirm FLR adequacy.  

3. Surgical resection  
   - Proceed to curative‑intent liver surgery: anatomic segmentectomy of segment III and non‑anatomic wedge resection of segment VI (or combined limited hepatectomy) aiming for R0 margins (≥1 mm).  
   - Intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion location and to detect any additional sub‑centimeter metastases.  
   - Preserve at least 30 % of functional liver parenchyma; no need for portal vein embolization given the small volume to be removed.  

4. Post‑operative (adjuvant) systemic therapy

Case_Content:
Man, 66 years old, right colectomy for T4N2M0 cancer 24 months ago. FDG-PET: four liver foci, 1.5-3.5 cm, no extra-hepatic. KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Multiple metachronous liver involvement, surgical feasibility to be discussed.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Category: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning:  
- Four hepatic lesions (1.5‑3.5 cm) are present, which is no longer an absolute contraindication to resection according to contemporary criteria.  
- No extra‑hepatic disease is identified on PET, satisfying the oncologic requirement for an R0 liver‑only approach.  
- Critical technical information is missing: precise segmental distribution (unilateral vs bilateral), proximity to major hepatic veins/portal pedicles, and calculated future liver remnant (FLR) volume. Without these data we cannot confirm that at least two contiguous liver segments with adequate inflow/outflow and an FLR ≥ 30 % (≥ 40 % after chemotherapy) can be preserved.  
- Because a decisive piece of information (anatomical feasibility/FLR) is lacking, the case must be classified as “Potentially resectable” pending further imaging and functional assessment.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
1. Baseline evaluation  
   - Obtain high‑quality triphasic CT or liver‑specific MRI with volumetry to define lesion locations, vascular relationships, and FLR.  
   - Perform liver function tests (bilirubin, albumin, INR), indocyanine‑green clearance if available, and assess performance status (ECOG/ASA).  
   - Measure serum CEA for baseline tumor marker.  

2. Systemic therapy (conversion/biologic assessment)  
   - Initiate 6 cycles of a fluoropyrimidine‑oxaliplatin doublet (e.g., FOLFOX) combined with anti‑VEGF (bevacizumab) given KRAS‑mutated status (anti‑EGFR agents are ineffective).  
   - Goal: (a) treat micrometastatic disease, (b) evaluate tumor biology (response vs progression), and (c) potentially downsize lesions.  

3. Restaging after chemotherapy  
   - Repeat liver MRI/CT with volumetry and PET‑CT to assess response, new lesions, and FLR.  
   - If disease is stable or responding and all lesions remain resectable, proceed to surgical planning.  

4. Surgical planning based on restaging  
   - If FLR ≥ 30 % (≥ 40 % after chemotherapy) and all lesions can be cleared in a single operation:  
     • Perform a curative‑intent hepatectomy (anatomical or non‑anatomical) aiming for R0 margins (≥ 1 mm).  
   - If FLR is insufficient or lesions are bilobar requiring extensive resection:  
     • Consider a two‑stage hepatectomy:  
       – Stage 1: Clear lesions from the future liver remnant (e.g., left lateral sectionectomy) and embolize the portal vein of the diseased lobe to induce hypertrophy.  
       – Interval of 4‑6 weeks with repeat imaging to confirm adequate hypertrophy.  
       – Stage 2: Resection of the hypertrophied remnant lobe.  
   - If a lesion is deep‑seated or near major vessels making resection risky:  
     • Combine limited resection with percutaneous ablation (RFA or microwave) to achieve complete local control while preserving parenchyma.  

5. Post‑operative management  
   - Resume adjuvant systemic therapy (additional 6‑8 cycles of FOLFOX‑bevacizumab) once recovery permits, to address microscopic disease.  
   - Schedule regular surveillance: CEA every 3 months, contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of the liver every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Detailed segmental location of each liver metastasis and their relationship to hepatic veins, portal branches, and bile ducts.  
- Quantified future liver remnant volume (percentage of total liver volume or FLR / body‑weight ratio).  
- Baseline liver function parameters (bilirubin, albumin, INR, ICG clearance if available).  
- Patient’s performance status and comorbidities (e.g., cardiovascular, pulmonary reserve).  
- Current serum CEA level.  
- Prior exposure to systemic chemotherapy (type, cycles) since the primary resection.  

These data are essential to move from “potentially resectable” to a definitive surgical plan.

Case_Content:
Woman, 71 years old, left colon cancer operated 5 years ago. Liver MRI: liver lesion segment V, 2.8 cm. CEA 90 ng/mL, RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Isolated metastasis, favorable context, good general condition.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront  
- Single metastasis, 2.8 cm, located in segment V – amenable to an anatomic segmentectomy or non‑anatomic wedge with clear margins.  
- No radiologically evident extra‑hepatic disease; MDT already describes the lesion as isolated.  
- Preservation of at least two contiguous liver segments is guaranteed; resection of segment V leaves >70 % of hepatic parenchyma, satisfying the ≥30 % future liver remnant (FLR) rule for a normal liver.  
- Patient is described as “good general condition,” indicating acceptable operative risk.  
Therefore, an R0 resection can be achieved immediately without prerequisite systemic therapy or additional information.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
1. Confirm staging before surgery  
   - Obtain a chest CT (or PET‑CT) to rule out occult pulmonary or other extra‑hepatic disease.  
   - Review baseline liver function tests, bilirubin, INR, albumin, and calculate FLR volumetry (CT‑based) to document adequacy.  
2. Surgical intervention (upfront)  
   - Perform a laparoscopic or open segment V resection (segmentectomy) aiming for ≥1 mm negative margin (R0).  
   - Use intra‑operative ultrasound to verify solitary disease and exclude additional occult lesions.  
   - Preserve inflow/outflow and biliary drainage of the remaining liver; ensure at least two contiguous segments remain.  
3. Post‑operative pathology  
   - Confirm R0 status, assess tumor grade, lymphovascular invasion, and margin width.  
4. Adjuvant systemic therapy (given RAS wild‑type and high pre‑operative CEA)  
   - Start 3–6 months of oxaliplatin‑based doublet (FOLFOX or CAPOX).  
   - Because the tumor is RAS wild‑type, add anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab) to the adjuvant regimen if tolerated, aiming to eradicate micrometastatic disease.  
5. Surveillance  
   - CEA measurement every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months up to 5 years.  
   - Contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (or CT) at 6 months post‑resection, then annually, or sooner if CEA rises.  
   - Continue multidisciplinary follow‑up to assess for recurrence and manage any new lesions promptly (re‑resection, ablation, or systemic therapy as appropriate).  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Detailed liver function panel (bilirubin, AST/ALT, INR, albumin) and quantitative FLR volumetry to document that the remnant will be ≥30 % of total liver volume.  
- Cardiopulmonary assessment (e.g., ECOG/ASA score, cardiology clearance) to confirm operative fitness.  
- Chest imaging (CT or PET‑CT) to definitively exclude pulmonary metastases.  
- Comorbidity burden (Charlson index or similar) and medication list to anticipate peri‑operative risk.  
- Pathologic details of the primary tumor (stage, lymph‑node status, margin status) that may influence adjuvant therapy intensity.

Case_Content:
Man, 64 years old, history of rectal resection (T3N1) 2 years ago. Liver MRI: two liver metastases, segments II and VIII, 2.5 and 3 cm. Thoracic CT scan negative for metastases. KRAS mutated, CEA 240 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Bilobar metachronous recurrence, technically accessible.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The two liver metastases (2.5 cm in segment II and 3 cm in segment VIII) are technically amenable to wedge resections with an expected future liver remnant >30 % and clear vascular inflow/outflow, satisfying the technical criteria for R0 resection. However, oncologic risk factors are unfavorable: metachronous disease with a very high pre‑operative CEA (240 ng/mL > 200 ng/mL) and KRAS mutation, both associated with higher recurrence risk. Current guidelines and the literature excerpts recommend neoadjuvant systemic therapy (“proof of time”) for patients with such adverse prognostic features before proceeding to curative surgery. Therefore, resection is contingent on completion of a defined pre‑operative chemotherapy course and reassessment of disease stability.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
• Initiate systemic chemotherapy promptly: preferred regimen is a doublet oxaliplatin‑based therapy (CAPOX or FOLFOX) combined with bevacizumab, given KRAS‑mutated status (anti‑EGFR agents are ineffective).  
• Plan for 4–6 cycles (approximately 2–3 months), monitoring CEA and repeat liver MRI (or contrast‑enhanced MRI) at the end of therapy to confirm radiologic response or stability and to re‑calculate future liver remnant.  
• If imaging shows no progression and the lesions remain resectable, proceed to a liver‑first (hepatectomy‑first) approach because the primary rectal tumor has already been resected and there is no evidence of extra‑hepatic disease.  
• Surgical plan: perform non‑anatomic wedge resections of segment II and segment VIII lesions (minor hepatectomy) via open or laparoscopic approach, preserving at least two contiguous segments and ensuring negative margins (≥1 mm, R0). No portal vein embolization is required given the small volume of resection.  
• Post‑operative management: resume systemic therapy (additional 3–6 cycles) as adjuvant treatment to address micrometastatic disease, given the high CEA and KRAS‑mutated biology.  
• Surveillance: CEA every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months; liver MRI or CT every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually, or earlier if CEA rises.

• Comorbidities (diabetes, cardiovascular disease) that could affect peri‑operative risk.

Case_Content:
Woman, 58 years old, left T4aN2M1 colon cancer with multiple bilobar metastases. After 6 cycles FOLFOX + bevacizumab: 60% volumetric reduction, CEA dropped from 880 to 180 ng/mL. Liver MRI: 5 remaining lesions, well-defined.
MDT Discussion: Major response to chemotherapy, surgical conversion considered.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – The current imaging shows five well‑defined bilobar lesions after a 60 % volumetric response to 6 cycles of FOLFOX + bevacizumab, and the primary colon tumor appears operable. However, definitive resectability cannot be confirmed without (a) a quantitative assessment of the future liver remnant (FLR) after planned parenchymal‑sparing or staged resections, and (b) confirmation that none of the lesions encroach critical vascular or biliary structures. These prerequisite evaluations are required before proceeding to surgery.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Continue systemic therapy for at most two additional cycles (total ≤ 8 cycles) to consolidate response, stopping bevacizumab at least 6 weeks before any hepatic operation to reduce wound‑healing complications.  
- Within 2 weeks after the last chemotherapy cycle, obtain:  
   • Triphasic CT or MRI with volumetric analysis to calculate FLR;  
   • Intra‑operative ultrasound‑guided mapping of all five lesions;  
   • Restaging PET/CT to exclude occult extra‑hepatic disease.  
- If FLR ≥ 30 % (normal liver) or ≥ 40 % (chemotherapy‑injured liver) and all lesions are amenable to parenchymal‑sparing resection (or limited non‑anatomic resections), plan a single‑stage combined colon and liver operation.  
- If FLR is insufficient, schedule portal vein embolization (PVE) or liver venous deprivation (LVD) to hypertrophy the remnant, re‑image after 2–4 weeks, and proceed to a staged hepatectomy (first stage: clearance of lesions in the future liver remnant, then PVE, then second‑stage major resection).  
- Perform the colon resection either simultaneously (if operative time and patient condition allow) or as a “reverse” approach (liver first, colon later) depending on symptomatology and oncologic urgency.  
- Post‑operative: resume systemic therapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) for a total of 6 months peri‑operatively (including any pre‑operative cycles already given). Consider adjuvant capecitabine‑oxaliplatin if the primary tumor was not previously resected with clear margins.  
- Enroll the patient in a multidisciplinary follow‑up schedule with CEA monitoring every 3 months and cross‑sectional imaging every 6 months for at least 3 years.

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Quantitative future liver remnant (FLR) volume after planned resections.  
- Exact size (maximum diameter) and precise segmental location of each hepatic lesion, including relationship to major vessels (hepatic veins, portal branches, hepatic artery).  
- Baseline and post‑chemotherapy liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count) and any evidence of chemotherapy‑associated liver injury (sinusoidal obstruction, steatohepatitis).  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and cardiopulmonary reserve.  
- Molecular profile of the primary tumor (KRAS, NRAS, BRAF, MSI status) to guide any further targeted therapy.  
- Confirmation of absence of extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum, distant nodes) on recent chest CT/PET‑CT.  
- Current status of the primary colon tumor (size, depth of invasion after chemotherapy, any obstruction or bleeding).  
- Planned surgical margin goals (R0 vs. R1 vascular resection) and willingness to perform vascular reconstruction if needed.

• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging every 3 months given the initially very high tumor burden.

Case_Content:
Man, 65 years old, sigmoid tumor with eight bilobar liver metastases. After 4 months FOLFIRI: radiological stability, CEA unchanged at 420 ng/mL. Thoracic CT scan negative for metastases.
MDT Discussion: Stable disease, not resectable, discussion on continuing systemic therapy.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has eight bilobar metastases, but no quantitative data on lesion size, segmental distribution, or future liver remnant (FLR) volume are provided. Without FLR assessment it is impossible to determine whether a curative hepatectomy (including possible two‑stage or ALPPS strategies) can be performed while preserving adequate liver function. Therefore the case meets the definition of “potentially resectable” because a decisive piece of information – volumetric FLR analysis (and related liver function assessment) – is missing.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Continue systemic therapy with a conversion‑intention regimen. Options:  
   • Switch to a more intensive doublet or triplet (e.g., FOLFOXIRI) combined with a biologic agent selected by molecular profile (anti‑EGFR if RAS wild‑type, anti‑VEGF otherwise).  
   • Maintain current FOLFIRI if tolerability is an issue, but add bevacizumab if not already present.  
- Re‑image the liver after 2–3 cycles (≈6–8 weeks) with contrast‑enhanced MRI or CT and repeat volumetric analysis to calculate FLR.  
- If tumor burden decreases and FLR ≥20‑30 % (adjusted for chemotherapy‑associated liver injury), proceed to surgical planning:  
   • For adequate FLR: consider a liver‑first approach with parenchymal‑sparing hepatectomy, aiming for R0 resection of all lesions.  
   • If FLR is insufficient but down‑staging has occurred: plan portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to hypertrophy the remnant.  
   • If disease remains bilobar with insufficient FLR after PVE, evaluate a two‑stage hepatectomy (resection of lesions in one lobe, then contralateral resection after hypertrophy).  
- Address the primary sigmoid tumor after hepatic disease is controlled:  
   • If the primary is asymptomatic, schedule sigmoid resection after liver surgery (either simultaneous if limited hepatectomy and patient fitness allow, or delayed).  
   • If symptoms develop (obstruction/bleeding), prioritize colorectal resection before or concurrently with liver surgery.  
- Throughout treatment, monitor CEA trends, performance status, and liver function tests; adjust systemic therapy for toxicity.  
- If after conversion attempts the disease progresses (new lesions, >3 lesions growing, or extra‑hepatic spread), shift to palliative systemic therapy and consider locoregional ablative options (RFA, SBRT) for residual liver disease.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Quantitative liver imaging: exact size of each metastasis, segmental location, and volumetric FLR calculation.  
- Liver function parameters: bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count, and assessment for chemotherapy‑associated liver injury.  
- Patient performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidities that affect surgical risk.  
- Molecular profile of the primary tumor (KRAS, NRAS, BRAF, MSI status) to guide biologic selection.  
- Detailed RECIST response assessment (percentage change in lesion size) to confirm true stability versus progression.  
- Baseline and trend of CEA beyond the single value reported, to help gauge tumor biology.  
- Assessment of portal venous anatomy and proximity of lesions to major vessels or biliary structures.

The patient presents with eight bilobar liver metastases and, after 4 months of FOLFIRI, shows radiological stability with persistently elevated CEA (420 ng/mL). The number of lesions, bilobar distribution, and absence of meaningful tumor downsizing make a complete R0 resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant not feasible. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is considered potentially resectable after major conversion.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Continuation and adaptation of systemic therapy
• Given the absence of radiologic response and stable high CEA, modification of the systemic regimen should be considered according to MDT discussion.
• The objective remains to achieve tumor downsizing sufficient to allow potential secondary resectability.

B. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2 months to detect any delayed response or change in lesion distribution.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

C. Criteria for reconsidering surgery
• Surgical re-evaluation can be considered only if a significant reduction in lesion size and number occurs, enabling parenchymal-sparing resections or multiples ablations or staged hepatectomy with adequate future liver remnant.

D. Alternative local strategies
• If systemic therapy achieves only partial control, consider alternative regimens (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution and vascular relationships of all eight lesions on MRI.
B. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation in case of potential future resection.
C. Molecular profile beyond current data to guide systemic therapy adaptation.
D. Status of the primary sigmoid tumor (resected or not).
E. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary rectal tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
E. Patient’s performance status and tolerance for ongoing systemic therapy.
F. Complete extrahepatic staging to confirm disease confinement to the liver.
G. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Woman, 49 years old, metastatic rectal cancer, ten initial liver lesions, CEA 1200 ng/mL. On FOLFOXIRI: disappearance of three foci, 40% reduction of others.Liver  MRI: several lesions became hypo-intense.

Response:

However, decisive information required to confirm technical resectability is missing: precise anatomic distribution of the residual lesions (bilobar vs. unilobar, proximity to major vessels or biliary structures), quantitative future liver remnant (FLR) volume, baseline liver function and any chemotherapy‑associated liver injury, and the presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease. Until these data are obtained, a definitive “Resectable upfront” or “Not resectable” classification cannot be made, making the case “Potentially resectable” pending further assessment.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Continue the current FOLFOXIRI regimen (or complete the planned number of cycles) to maximize tumor shrinkage and to use response as a biological test of disease aggressiveness.  
- At the end of the neoadjuvant phase (typically after 6–8 cycles, ≈2–3 months), repeat high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast and obtain a contrast‑enhanced CT for volumetric analysis.  
- Perform a dedicated liver volumetry study to calculate FLR; if FLR < 30 % in the setting of chemotherapy‑injured liver (or < 20 % in a normal liver), plan portal vein embolization (PVE) or consider a two‑stage hepatectomy/ALPPS to induce hypertrophy.  
- Simultaneously reassess the rectal primary: if symptomatic (bleeding, obstruction) or high‑risk T4 disease, schedule neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy followed by primary resection; if asymptomatic, a liver‑first approach is acceptable.  
- Multidisciplinary review of the updated imaging to map each residual metastasis; aim for an R0 resection while preserving at least two contiguous liver segments with adequate inflow/outflow and biliary drainage.  
- If all lesions can be cleared with adequate FLR, proceed to curative‑intent hepatic resection (potentially extended right or left hepatectomy, or combined segmental resections) possibly combined with intra‑operative ablation for lesions in difficult locations.  
- Post‑operative plan: 3–6 months of adjuvant systemic therapy (FOLFOXIRI or a doublet plus targeted agent based on molecular profile) and, if indicated, postoperative pelvic radiotherapy for the rectal primary.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Quantitative future liver remnant volume and liver volumetry data.  
- Exact segmental location of each residual liver lesion and relationship to hepatic veins, portal pedicles, and biliary ducts.  
- Baseline liver function tests and assessment of chemotherapy‑associated liver injury (e.g., steatosis, sinusoidal obstruction).  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic metastases (lung, peritoneum, lymph nodes).  
- Performance status and comorbidities influencing surgical risk.  
- Molecular profile of the tumor (RAS, BRAF, MSI) to guide targeted therapy decisions.  
- Details of the rectal primary (T stage, nodal status, symptoms, prior radiotherapy).

The patient initially presented with ten liver metastases. This situation is therefore considered potentially resectable after conversion therapy, pending detailed re-evaluation.

• Perform high-quality liver MRI with diffusion sequences and compare meticulously with pre-treatment imaging and a chest CT scan.
• Identify the exact locations of the three “disappeared” metastases, as these sites may still harbor viable microscopic disease.

• Determine whether all initial metastatic sites (not only visible residual lesions) can be encompassed within a surgical plan using parenchymal-sparing resections, staged hepatectomy, or combined resection/ablation.

• If all initial sites can be addressed, proceed with an ultrasound-guided parenchymal-sparing strategy, potentially in staged fashion depending on FLR.
• The objective is removal or ablation of every original metastatic location.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.

D. If complete clearance is not achievable
• Continue systemic therapy and reassess after additional cycles.

Case_Content:
Man, 71 years old, metastatic right colon cancer (KRAS mutated). After 8 cycles FOLFOX: progression of two lesions segment VII and VIII (up to 5.2 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 950 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Progression on chemotherapy, no surgical window at this stage.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – The two hepatic lesions in segments VII and VIII are technically amenable to a curative‑intent resection (segmentectomy or limited right posterior resection) provided an adequate future liver remnant can be preserved. However, disease progression while on optimal first‑line FOLFOX demonstrates aggressive tumor biology and indicates that surgery cannot be performed now. A prerequisite action – achievement of disease control with second‑line systemic therapy (or an effective locoregional modality) – must be completed before a surgical attempt can be justified.  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Switch to second‑line chemotherapy appropriate for KRAS‑mutated disease: FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab (anti‑VEGF) is the standard choice after FOLFOX failure.  
- Administer 2–3 cycles and restage with triphasic CT (or MRI with hepatobiliary contrast) to assess RECIST response and CEA trend.  
- If imaging shows tumor shrinkage or at least stable disease and CEA declines, proceed to multidisciplinary re‑evaluation of resectability.  
- Evaluate functional liver reserve: obtain liver function tests, indocyanine‑green clearance (if available), and calculate FLR volume. If FLR is <30 % (or <40 % after prior chemotherapy), consider portal vein embolization to hypertrophy the left liver before resection.  
- Surgical plan (once disease control is confirmed):  
   • Perform a right posterior sectorectomy (segments VII‑VIII) aiming for R0 margins (>1 mm).  
   • Preserve at least two contiguous left‑liver segments (II–IV) with adequate inflow/outflow and biliary drainage.  
   • If the primary right‑colon tumor has not yet been resected and is asymptomatic, schedule a staged or simultaneous colectomy based on patient fitness and operative risk; otherwise, treat the primary with surgery after hepatic control.  
- If second‑line chemotherapy fails (progression or new lesions), shift to locoregional therapies:  
   • Y‑90 radio‑embolization or hepatic arterial infusion pump chemotherapy to achieve local disease control.  
   • Percutaneous thermal ablation (RFA or microwave) or stereotactic body radiotherapy for lesions ≤3 cm if they become amenable.  
- Continue systemic therapy (maintenance FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) after any local treatment, and monitor CEA and imaging every 8–12 weeks.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Current status of the primary colon tumor (resected, unresected, symptomatic).  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG), comorbidities, and cardiopulmonary reserve to tolerate major liver surgery.  
- Detailed liver function tests (bilirubin, albumin, INR, ICG clearance) and quantitative future liver remnant volume.  
- Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum, lymph nodes) on recent thoraco‑abdominal imaging.  
- Whether anti‑VEGF therapy was included in the initial FOLFOX regimen and the exact RECIST measurements of the two lesions before and after chemotherapy.  
- Baseline nutritional status and frailty assessment given the patient’s age (71 y).
Reference:

The patient shows progression of liver disease under FOLFOX with enlargement of two lesions in segments VII and VIII (up to 5.2 cm) and markedly elevated CEA (950 ng/mL). This radiologic progression under systemic therapy indicates biologically aggressive disease and makes a complete R0 resection with adequate oncologic control not achievable at this stage. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this situation is considered unresectable in the current setting.

A. Adaptation of systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Given progression on FOLFOX, a change of systemic regimen is required according to MDT decision (e.g., switch to FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab).
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.

• Perform high-resolution liver MRI every 2 months to evaluate response to the new regimen.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

C. Criteria for reconsidering surgery
• Surgical re-evaluation can be considered only if a significant radiologic response occurs, allowing parenchymal-sparing resection with adequate future liver remnant.

D. If disease remains progressive
• Continue systemic therapy and consider alternative regimens (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor).
• Consider local palliative approaches if needed according to MDT.

A. Exact segmental distribution and vascular relationships of all liver lesions on MRI.
B. Status of the primary colon tumor (resected or not).
C. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary rectal tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
E. Presence or absence of extrahepatic disease on full restaging.

Case_Content:
Woman, 62 years old, left colon adenocarcinoma with seven liver metastases. After 6 cycles FOLFOX + panitumumab: complete disappearance of four foci and reduction of others at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA normalized.
MDT Discussion: Radiological complete response in several segments, uncertainty regarding microscopic persistence.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
- The patient has responded dramatically to 6 cycles of FOLFOX + panitumumab with radiologic disappearance of four hepatic lesions and reduction of the remaining three, but the exact size, location and volumetric impact of the residual disease are not provided.  
- Definitive resectability requires (a) confirmation that all known disease sites—including the sites of radiologic complete response—can be removed with negative margins, and (b) assurance that the future liver remnant (FLR) will be ≥30 % (or ≥20 % in a normal liver) with adequate inflow/outflow and biliary drainage. Both of these criteria are currently missing, making the case “potentially resectable” pending further information.  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
1. Restaging and planning  
   - Obtain a high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast (or contrast‑enhanced CT) to delineate the exact anatomy of the residual lesions and to locate the scar tissue of the disappeared lesions.  
   - Perform volumetric analysis to calculate FLR; if FLR < 30 % consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy.  
   - Review colon primary: if not yet resected, schedule definitive left‑sided colectomy (extended left hemicolectomy) in the same operative session if the patient’s performance status permits.  

2. Surgical approach  
   - Plan a parenchymal‑sparing liver resection targeting the three residual metastases (e.g., non‑anatomic wedge resections or segmental resections) and resect the original sites of the four lesions that have radiologically disappeared, guided by intra‑operative ultrasound and, when necessary, indocyanine‑green fluorescence to identify scar tissue.  
   - Aim for R0 margins (>1 mm) while preserving at least two contiguous functional liver segments with intact portal/arterial inflow and hepatic venous outflow.  
   - If FLR is insufficient after planned resections, proceed with pre‑operative PVE, re‑image after hypertrophy (≈4–6 weeks), and then perform a staged liver resection followed by colon resection (or vice‑versa) depending on intra‑operative findings.  

3. Peri‑operative systemic therapy  
   - Stop panitumumab at least 5 weeks before surgery to reduce wound‑healing complications (as suggested by bevacizumab data; similar interval is prudent for EGFR antibodies).  
   - After complete resection, deliver adjuvant FOLFOX (or CAPOX) for 6 months; EGFR‑targeted therapy is not routinely added in the adjuvant setting for resected CLM.  
   - Continue regular surveillance: CEA every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months; cross‑sectional imaging (CT or MRI) of chest/abdomen every 6 months for 2 years, then annually.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Precise volumetric measurement of future liver remnant (FLR) and liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count).  
- Exact size, number and segmental location of the three residual metastases after chemotherapy.  
- Confirmation of the status of the primary left‑colon tumor (resected vs. still in situ) and its staging (T/N).  
- KRAS/NRAS/BRAF mutation status (panitumumab use implies wild‑type KRAS, but full RAS/BRAF profile is needed).  
- Patient’s performance status, cardiopulmonary reserve, and comorbidities that could affect surgical risk.  
- Evidence of any extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum) on recent chest/abdomen/pelvis imaging.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially had seven liver metastases. After 6 cycles of FOLFOX + panitumumab, four lesions have radiologically disappeared and the remaining lesions have significantly decreased in size, with normalization of CEA. Despite this excellent response, the initial tumor burden and the phenomenon of “disappearing metastases” mean that viable microscopic disease may persist at the original sites. This situation is therefore considered potentially resectable after conversion therapy, but requires meticulous mapping of all initial metastatic locations before surgery.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with diffusion sequences and systematically compare with pre-treatment imaging.
• Precisely localize all initial metastatic sites, including those no longer visible.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Surgical strategy addressing initial disease map
• Plan a parenchymal-sparing, ultrasound-guided surgical approach that includes resection or ablation of all initial metastatic locations, not only residual visible lesions.
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential to identify occult residual disease.
• Depending on lesion distribution, this may require a staged approach.

C. Management of the primary tumor
• Left colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for primary cancer resection.
• A staged approach with colectomy first is preferred.

D. Postoperative systemic therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Resume systemic therapy after surgery to complete approximately 6 months of total treatment.

E. If complete surgical clearance of all initial sites is not feasible
• Continue systemic therapy and reassess, or consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal approach.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial lesions on baseline imaging.
B. Precise localization of the four “disappeared” metastases.
C. Detailed vascular and biliary relationships of remaining lesions.
D. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
E. Status of the primary colon tumor (resected or not).
G. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary rectal tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Man, 55 years old, metastatic rectal cancer (RAS wild-type), ten initial liver lesions. After 4 cycles of chemotherapy,liver MRI: three residual lesions <2 cm, CEA decreased from 1100 to 80 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Major response, potentially curative situation to be surgically re-evaluated.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Category: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning: The post‑chemotherapy MRI shows three residual metastases each <2 cm, which from a purely oncologic view could be amenable to curative‑intent resection. However, technical feasibility cannot be confirmed without decisive information that is currently missing:  

- Precise segmental location of each lesion and their relationship to the hepatic veins, portal pedicles and biliary structures (needed to guarantee an R0 margin while preserving at least two contiguous liver segments).  
- Quantitative assessment of the future liver remnant (FLR) volume or FLR/body‑weight ratio (>30 % or >0.5 % respectively) to ensure adequate postoperative liver function.  

Because these data are essential to determine whether a safe, margin‑negative hepatectomy can be performed, the case must be classified as “Potentially resectable” pending further evaluation (or a prerequisite intervention such as portal vein embolization if FLR proves insufficient).

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  

- Continue systemic therapy to complete a standard peri‑operative course (e.g., total 6 – 8 cycles of a doublet regimen such as FOLFOX or FOLFIRI combined with anti‑EGFR antibody given RAS‑wild‑type status). This consolidates tumor response and provides additional “proof of time” for disease biology.  
- At cycle 6 (or earlier if imaging suggests maximal response), repeat high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast and obtain a volumetric CT to:  
   • Re‑map lesion locations, confirm absence of new intra‑ or extra‑hepatic disease (including chest CT).  
   • Calculate FLR; if FLR <30 % consider pre‑operative portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy to induce hypertrophy.  
- If imaging confirms that all three lesions can be resected with negative margins while preserving adequate FLR, schedule curative‑intent liver surgery. Preferred approach: anatomic or non‑anatomic resections tailored to lesion distribution, using intra‑operative ultrasound to detect any occult disease.  
- Simultaneously address the primary rectal tumor: if the rectal lesion is still in situ and resectable, plan a combined or staged colorectal resection (e.g., low anterior resection with total mesorectal excision) after liver surgery, depending on patient fitness and operative risk.  
- Post‑operative management:  
   • Pathologic assessment of resection margins; if R0 achieved, proceed with adjuvant systemic therapy (e.g., 3–6 months of the same doublet ± biologic) to eradicate micrometastatic disease.  
   • Monitor CEA and imaging every 3–4 months for the first 2 years, then semi‑annually.  

Step 3 – Missing data  

- Exact segmental location of each hepatic lesion and proximity to major vessels/biliary structures.  
- Quantitative future liver remnant volume (or FLR/body‑weight ratio).  
- Baseline liver function tests and indocyanine‑green clearance (if available) to assess hepatic reserve.  
- Performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidity profile (e.g., cardiovascular, pulmonary).  
- Status of the primary rectal tumor (already resected, in situ, symptomatic) and any local staging (MRI pelvis).  
- Comprehensive extra‑hepatic staging (chest CT/PET‑CT) to rule out pulmonary or peritoneal disease.  
- Molecular profile beyond RAS (BRAF, MSI/dMMR) which may influence adjuvant choices.  

These items are essential to finalize resectability and to tailor the definitive surgical plan.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient initially presented with ten liver metastases. After 4 cycles of chemotherapy, MRI shows only three residual lesions <2 cm and a major biologic response (CEA from 1100 to 80 ng/mL). Despite this marked response, the initial tumor burden and likely bilobar distribution require careful mapping of all original metastatic sites. This situation is considered resectable, pending detailed segmental and volumetric reassessment.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Mandatory expert restaging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI with diffusion sequences and meticulous comparison with baseline imaging. Perform a chest CT scan to assess extrahepatic disease.
• Precisely localize all initial metastatic sites, including those no longer visible (“disappeared metastases”).
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

B. Surgical strategy based on the initial disease map
• If technically feasible, plan a parenchymal-sparing, ultrasound-guided approach aiming to resect or ablate all original metastatic locations, not only the three visible lesions.
• Depending on distribution and FLR, this may require a staged hepatectomy.
• The objective is removal or ablation of every original metastatic location.
• Aim for R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

C. Integration with rectal primary management
• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles (PRODIGE 23 protocol).
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvic MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : strict follow up of primary tumor + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery: oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles) + resection or ablation of the remaining lesions
• Coordinate pelvic treatment and timing of rectal surgery with the hepatic surgical plan according to rectal oncologic principles.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

D. Postoperative systemic therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Resume systemic therapy after surgery to complete approximately 6 months of total treatment.

E. If complete clearance of all initial sites is not achievable
• Continue systemic therapy and reassess, or consider local ablative techniques as part of a multimodal approach.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution of all initial and residual lesions on pre- and post-chemotherapy MRI and precise localization of the “disappeared” metastases.
B. Detailed vascular and biliary relationships of residual lesions.
D. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
E. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary rectal tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
F. Status and treatment plan of the rectal primary tumor : Circumferential resection margin (CRM) status on pelvic MRI, essential for rectal surgical planning. Exact distance of the rectal tumor from the anal verge, influencing the type of rectal resection and anastomotic risk.
G. Perform a chest CT scan to assess extrahepatic disease
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Woman, 67 years old, T4N2M1 transverse colon cancer, multiple bilobar liver metastases, CEA 600 ng/mL. On FOLFOX: overall stability, two new lesions detected at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan.
MDT Discussion: Limited progression on treatment, question of changing protocol.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has multiple bilobar liver metastases and has shown limited progression on FOLFOX with two new lesions on recent imaging, indicating that the current systemic therapy is not achieving disease control. Definitive determination of technical resectability cannot be made without critical information such as the exact number, size, and vascular relationship of each hepatic lesion, the calculated future liver remnant (FLR) volume, and the status of the newly identified extra‑hepatic lesions (presumed lung). Moreover, the tumor’s molecular profile (RAS/BRAF status) is needed to select an optimal conversion regimen. Because these data are missing and a conversion strategy (e.g., intensified chemotherapy, targeted agents, or locoregional liver‑directed therapy) must be attempted before surgery, the case falls into the “Potentially resectable” category.

- Obtain comprehensive restaging: high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast and a dedicated chest CT or PET‑CT to define all hepatic and extra‑hepatic disease.  
- Perform molecular profiling of the primary tumor (RAS, BRAF, MSI‑H) and repeat baseline liver function tests, bilirubin, INR, and platelet count.  
- Switch systemic therapy because of progression on FOLFOX:  
   • If RAS wild‑type and BRAF wild‑type, initiate a triplet regimen (FOLFOXIRI) plus an anti‑EGFR antibody (cetuximab or panitumumab).  
   • If RAS mutated or anti‑EGFR contraindicated, consider FOLFIRI + bevacizumab or a switch to a different doublet (FOLFIRI + bevacizumab).  
- Re‑evaluate after 2–3 months (minimum 4 cycles) with imaging; assess response using RECIST and tumor markers (CEA trend).  
- If disease stabilises or shrinks:  
   • Re‑calculate FLR using volumetric CT/MRI; if FLR ≥ 30 % (or >0.5 % body‑weight ratio) proceed to surgical planning.  
   • For borderline FLR, consider portal vein embolisation (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy (TSH) with clearance of the future liver remnant in the first stage, followed by hypertrophy induction and second‑stage resection.  
   • If lesions are centrally located or involve major vessels, evaluate parenchymal‑sparing resections, possible R1 vascular resection, or adjunctive intra‑operative ablation.

- Exact number, maximal diameter, and segmental distribution of all liver metastases.  
- Relationship of hepatic lesions to major vascular structures (portal/hepatic veins, hepatic artery).  
- Calculated future liver remnant volume and functional liver reserve (e.g., indocyanine‑green clearance if available).  
- Detailed status of the two new lesions on thoraco‑abdominal CT (size, organ involved, resectability).  
- Molecular profile of the tumor (RAS, BRAF, MSI‑H).  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG), comorbidities, and baseline liver function tests.  
- Pulmonary function tests if lung metastasectomy is contemplated.
