• Start systemic doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± anti-EGFR given RAS wild-type status).
• The objective is to assess tumor biology and confirm disease control at hepatic and pulmonary sites.

C. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver and pelvic MRI, and thoraco-abdominal enhanced CT-scan every 2-3 months to evaluate response and detect any potential reduction in tumor burden that could open a limited local treatment window.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

D. Criteria for secondary resectability
• Surgery can be considered only if chemotherapy induces:
– Significant reduction in lesion size and number in both liver and lung.
– Feasibility of staged or parenchymal-sparing resections with adequate future liver remnant.

E. Potential surgical strategies for liver metastases if response is favorable
• Two-stage hepatectomy or combined parenchymal-sparing resections depending on response pattern.
• Portal vein embolization / venous deprivation / ALPPS may be required if major hepatectomy becomes necessary.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

F. Management of the rectal primary
• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy with chemotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles (PRODIGE 23 protocol).
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvic MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : strict follow up of primary tumor
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery: oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles).
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

G. Management of the single lung metastase
• Plan pulmonary metastasectomy or ablative treatment in a staged manner.
• Preoperative evaluation of respiratory function

I. If insufficient response and if disease remains disseminated
• Continue second-line systemic therapy or adapt regimen (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor) according to MDT, with possible consideration of local ablative techniques.
• Continue systemic third-line chemotherapy and consider palliative or symptom-oriented strategies according to MDT.

J. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging of both liver and lungs.

A. Exact segmental distribution and vascular relationships of the liver metastases.
B. Resectability assessment of the lung lesion by thoracic surgery.
C. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
D. Detailed pelvic MRI to plan rectal treatment.
E. Patient’s performance status for staged multimodal procedures.
F. Confirmation of absence of other extrahepatic disease on full staging.
G. Evolution of CEA and radiologic response over time.

Case_Content:
Man, 62 years old, left colon cancer with six liver metastases and lymph node involvement of the hepatic pedicle at the abdominal CT scan. KRAS mutated, CEA 780 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Liver involvement associated with extra-hepatic lymph nodes, unfavorable prognosis.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
- Six hepatic metastases (multiple, likely bilobar) and radiologically evident hepatic‑pedicle lymph node metastasis place the case beyond immediate R0 resection.  
- Current imaging does not provide: (a) precise distribution of the lesions relative to major vascular inflow/outflow, (b) volumetric assessment of future liver remnant, (c) size and exact anatomic location of the hilar nodes (hepatoduodenal‑retropancreatic vs. common hepatic artery region).  
- Because a definitive determination of whether an R0 resection with adequate FLR is feasible requires down‑staging and further staging work‑up, the case meets the definition of “Potentially resectable” (prerequisite: neoadjuvant systemic therapy with response assessment and detailed volumetric imaging).

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Initiate conversion systemic chemotherapy: FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab (KRAS‑mutated disease precludes anti‑EGFR agents).  
- Re‑stage after 2–3 months (or after 4–6 cycles) with contrast‑enhanced liver MRI (or triphasic CT) plus PET‑CT to (i) quantify tumor response, (ii) delineate residual disease, (iii) reassess hepatic‑pedicle nodal burden, and (iv) calculate FLR.  
- If imaging shows ≥ 30 % FLR in a healthy liver (or ≥ 40 % if chemotherapy‑associated liver injury is present) and all lesions appear resectable with negative margins, proceed to surgical planning:  
   • Consider a liver‑first approach because the primary left‑sided colon tumor is asymptomatic; resect hepatic disease first.  
   • If FLR is insufficient, schedule portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to induce hypertrophy, followed by second‑stage resection.  
   • For the hepatic‑pedicle nodes, perform limited lymphadenectomy if they are confined to the hepatoduodenal‑retropancreatic zone and can be removed with clear margins; gross involvement of the common hepatic artery/celiac axis nodes would contraindicate hepatic resection.  
   • After hepatic clearance, perform definitive left‑colectomy (laparoscopic or open) either simultaneously (if liver resection is limited) or in a second operation, depending on operative risk and patient fitness.  
- Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy (same regimen or maintenance) for at least 3–6 months, with close CEA monitoring and imaging surveillance every 3–4 months.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Patient performance status (ECOG/ASA) and comorbidities.  
- Baseline liver function tests and presence of chemotherapy‑associated liver injury.  
- Detailed size, exact segmental location, and vascular relationship of each of the six liver metastases.  
- Quantitative future liver remnant volume (CT/MRI volumetry).  
- Precise anatomic extent of hepatic‑pedicle lymph node involvement (size, laterality, relation to hepatic artery/portal vein).  
- Presence or absence of other extra‑hepatic sites (lung, peritoneum) on chest CT/PET‑CT.  
- Baseline tumor biology beyond KRAS (e.g., BRAF, MSI status).  
- Symptoms from the primary colon tumor (obstruction, bleeding).
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with six liver metastases associated with lymph node involvement of the hepatic pedicle. The presence of extrahepatic nodal disease at the hepatic hilum reflects systemic dissemination and markedly unfavorable tumor biology. Even if the liver lesions were technically resectable, the oncologic context precludes a curative hepatobiliary surgical approach at this stage. This situation is therefore considered potentially resectable from a hepatobiliary perspective.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Comprehensive staging and multidisciplinary planning
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and thoraco-abdominal CT to confirm exact number, distribution, and resectability of liver lesions and other para-aortic enlarged lymph nodes and a chest CT scan
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).
• Given the high CEA level (780 ng/mL) and multifocal metastases, perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Systemic therapy as primary strategy (mandatory)
• Initiate or adapt systemic chemotherapy according to MDT decision (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab;
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR).
• The objective is global disease control and assessment of tumor biology.

C. Radiologic reassessment after treatment
• Perform high-quality liver MRI and abdominal CT after 2–3 months to reassess liver disease and nodal involvement.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of response.

D. Criteria for reconsidering surgery (highly exceptional)
• Surgical re-evaluation could be considered only in case of major response with major regression of nodal disease and significant downsizing of liver lesions.
• Any surgical strategy would remain highly selected and dependent on sustained disease control.

E. Surgical management of liver metastases (parenchymal-sparing strategy)
• If stability or response is observed, perform multiple wedge/segmental resections or ablation guided by intra-operative ultrasound:
• The goal is R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma and avoiding major hepatectomy.
• Perform en-bloc lymphadenectomy of the hepatic pedicles 
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

F. Management of the primary tumor
• If the sigmoid tumor has not yet been resected, a simultaneous sigmoid colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis can be considered, provided the patient’s condition allows combined surgery.
• Otherwise, a staged approach with colectomy first is acceptable.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for primary cancer resection.

G. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging of both liver and lungs.

Case_Content:
Woman, 70 years old, right T4N2M1 colon cancer, multiple bilobar liver metastases and a single cerebellar metastasis at the total body CT scan. CEA 860 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Systemic disease with brain involvement, neurological priority indication.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has multiple bilobar liver metastases and a single cerebellar metastasis. Current imaging shows extra‑hepatic disease (brain) that must be controlled before any curative‑intent liver surgery. Moreover, the burden of liver disease is not yet quantified for future liver remnant (FLR) adequacy, and systemic disease biology is unknown. Therefore resection cannot be performed upfront; it will become feasible only after (a) definitive treatment of the cerebellar lesion and (b) systemic therapy to assess response and possibly downsize hepatic disease, allowing a safe R0 hepatectomy with adequate FLR.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Immediate management of the cerebellar metastasis:  
   • If symptomatic or causing mass effect, neurosurgical resection; otherwise stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) is preferred for a solitary lesion.  
- Obtain molecular profile of the primary tumor (RAS, BRAF, MSI/MMR) and baseline performance status (ECOG), liver function tests, and calculate FLR (CT volumetry or MRI).  
- Initiate systemic chemotherapy tailored to molecular status (e.g., FOLFOXIRI ± anti‑VEGF for RAS‑wild type, or appropriate doublet + biologic for RAS‑mutated disease). Give 2–3 months (≈ 4–6 cycles) while monitoring CEA trend.  
- Restage after chemotherapy with high‑resolution liver MRI, contrast‑enhanced CT of chest/abdomen, and repeat brain imaging to confirm control of the cerebellar lesion.  
- If liver disease responds sufficiently and FLR ≥30 % (or ≥0.5 %/kg body weight), plan curative hepatic resection:  
   • Consider a two‑stage hepatectomy or portal vein embolization if FLR is borderline.  
   • Aim for R0 resection of all hepatic lesions; use intra‑operative ultrasound to guide.  
- After hepatic surgery, address the primary right‑sided colon tumor:  
   • If the patient’s postoperative course is uncomplicated and the primary is asymptomatic, perform a right hemicolectomy in a delayed (sequential) fashion; simultaneous resection may be considered only if the liver operation is limited and the patient’s physiologic reserve permits.  
- Continue postoperative (adjuvant) systemic therapy for at least 6 months, adjusting based on response and tolerability.  
- Implement a surveillance schedule: CEA every 3 months, cross‑sectional imaging of liver and chest every 6 months, and brain MRI annually or as clinically indicated.

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Molecular profile of the tumor (RAS, BRAF, MSI/MMR).  
- Exact number, maximal diameter, and vascular proximity of each liver metastasis.  
- Quantified future liver remnant volume.  
- Detailed neurologic status and size/location of the cerebellar lesion to decide between surgery vs. radiosurgery.  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG), comorbidities, and cardiopulmonary reserve.  
- Baseline liver function (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count).  
- Planned systemic regimen and any prior chemotherapy exposure.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with multiple bilobar liver metastases associated with a cerebellar metastasis in the context of a right T4N2 colon cancer and markedly elevated CEA (860 ng/mL). The presence of brain metastasis indicates advanced systemic dissemination and excludes any curative hepatobiliary surgical strategy at this stage. From a hepatobiliary perspective, this situation is considered unresectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Neurological priority (mandatory)
• Immediate neurosurgical and/or radiotherapy assessment of the cerebellar metastasis is required as the first therapeutic step.
• The objective is neurological control and symptom prevention.

B. Comprehensive staging and multidisciplinary planning
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and thoraco-abdominal CT to confirm exact number, distribution, and resectability of liver lesions
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).
• Given the high CEA level (860 ng/mL) and multifocal metastases, perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

C. Systemic therapy after neurological stabilization
• Initiate or adapt systemic chemotherapy according to MDT decision once neurological status is stabilized.
• The objective is global disease control.

D. Radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-quality liver MRI and full-body imaging after 2–3 months to evaluate response.
• Monitor CEA kinetics.

E. Criteria for reconsidering liver-directed therapy (exceptional)
• Hepatobiliary surgical re-evaluation would be considered only in the rare situation of complete neurological control and major hepatic response, which remains highly unlikely.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Neurological status and resectability of the cerebellar metastasis.
B. Exact segmental distribution and vascular relationships of liver lesions.
D. Molecular profile to optimize systemic treatment.
E. Status and symptoms related to the primary colon tumor.
F. Presence or absence of additional extrahepatic disease on full staging.

Case_Content:
Man, 55 years old, rectosigmoid tumor, four liver metastases and pelvic peritoneal implants at the abdominal CT scan. BRAF wild-type, CEA 320 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Hepato-peritoneal involvement, possible multimodal strategy to be discussed.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Category: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning:  
- Four hepatic metastases (likely bilobar) can be technically resected if an adequate future liver remnant (≥30 % of total liver volume) can be preserved; this information is not provided.  
- Pelvic peritoneal implants represent extra‑hepatic disease. Limited peritoneal disease may be amenable to cytoreductive surgery ± HIPEC, but the extent (PCI score, number and size of implants) is unknown.  
- The primary rectosigmoid lesion is not described as symptomatic or obstructive; its resectability and need for neoadjuvant radiotherapy are not stated.  
- High CEA (320 ng/mL) and synchronous disease are unfavorable biologic criteria that usually prompt a neoadjuvant systemic approach (“proof of time”) before committing to surgery.  
Because a specific prerequisite (systemic chemotherapy to assess disease biology and downsize liver lesions, and a detailed peritoneal disease assessment) is required before a definitive surgical plan, the case fits the “Potentially resectable” category.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy (step‑by‑step)  
1. Baseline work‑up  
   - Full performance‑status assessment (ECOG), comorbidity review (ASA, cardiac/pulmonary reserve).  
   - High‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast and diffusion‑weighted sequences to define size, location, vascular involvement of each metastasis and to calculate future liver remnant (FLR).  
   - Pelvic MRI and/or diagnostic laparoscopy to map peritoneal implants, assign a Peritoneal Cancer Index (PCI), and confirm that complete cytoreduction is feasible.  
   - Colonoscopy with biopsy of the rectosigmoid primary; assess need for pre‑operative radiotherapy (low‑rectal location).  

2. Systemic induction therapy (first 3–4 months)  
   - Preferred regimen: FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab (intensive double‑/triplet chemotherapy given high tumor burden and CEA).  
   - Monitor response with RECIST criteria after every 2 cycles; repeat CEA to gauge biologic response.  

3. Restaging after induction  
   - Repeat liver MRI and pelvic imaging.  
   - If hepatic disease shows ≥30 % reduction in total tumor volume and FLR is now ≥30 % (or can be achieved with portal vein embolization), proceed to hepatic surgery.  
   - If peritoneal disease remains limited (PCI ≤10–12) and resectable, schedule cytoreductive surgery with HIPEC.  

4. Surgical sequencing (tailored to response and patient fitness)  
   - Option A – Liver‑first strategy (preferred when liver disease is the dominant threat):  
        a. Portal vein embolization (PVE) if FLR insufficient.  
        b. Two‑stage hepatectomy or single‑stage major hepatectomy achieving R0 resection of all liver lesions.  
        c. After hepatic recovery (4–6 weeks), proceed to definitive rectosigmoid resection (low anterior resection or APR) and peritoneal cytoreduction ± HIPEC in the same operation if operative risk acceptable.  
   - Option B – Simultaneous approach (if FLR adequate, primary tumor low‑rectal without need for long‑course radiotherapy, and peritoneal disease limited):  
        a. Combined colorectal resection and liver resection in one operation, followed by intra‑operative HIPEC for peritoneal implants.  
   - Option C – Delayed primary (if primary tumor requires radiotherapy or is symptomatic):  
        a. Complete hepatic resection first, then short‑course pelvic radiotherapy, then definitive colorectal surgery and peritoneal cytoreduction.  

5. Adjuvant therapy  
   - Post‑operative systemic chemotherapy (6–8 cycles) tailored to residual disease and molecular profile (RAS status pending).  
   - Consider targeted agents (anti‑EGFR if RAS wild‑type) after recovery.  

6. Surveillance  
   - CEA every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months.  
   - Contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of chest/abdomen/pelvis every 6 months for 3 years, then annually.  

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Performance status (ECOG/ASA) and cardiopulmonary comorbidities.  
- Detailed liver imaging (MRI) to calculate future liver remnant volume and vascular anatomy.  
- Exact distribution (segmental location) of the four liver metastases.  
- Peritoneal disease burden: number, size, PCI score, and feasibility of complete cytoreduction.  
- Resectability of the rectosigmoid primary (distance from anal verge, involvement of adjacent organs, need for pre‑operative radiotherapy).  
- RAS mutation status and microsatellite instability status (to guide targeted/immune therapy).  
- Baseline liver function tests and serum albumin (to assess risk of postoperative liver failure).
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with four liver metastases associated with pelvic peritoneal implants in the setting of a rectosigmoid tumor. The presence of peritoneal carcinomatosis indicates extrahepatic dissemination and precludes a standard curative hepatobiliary surgical approach at this stage. From a hepatobiliary perspective, this situation is considered potentially resectable in the current setting.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Comprehensive staging and multidisciplinary planning
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT to confirm exact number, distribution, and resectability of both liver and peritoneal lesions and a chest CT scan.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).
• Given the high CEA level (320 ng/mL) and multifocal metastases, perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Induction systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Administer 2–3 months of peri-operative doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) according to MDT decision to assess tumor biology and optimize oncologic control according to patient tolerance.
• This allows treatment of potential micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology before surgery.
• The goal is to evaluate tumor biology and potential response at both hepatic and peritoneal sites.

C. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and thoraco-abdominal enhanced CT-scan every 2-3 months to evaluate response and detect any potential reduction in tumor burden that could open a limited local treatment window.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

D. Criteria for reconsidering surgical strategy
• Surgical re-evaluation may be considered only in the rare situation of major response with near-complete control of peritoneal disease and limited residual liver lesions.
• If disease control or response is observed:
	1.	Perform parenchymal-sparing liver resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound : 
• Intra-operative ultrasound is essential to guide both resection and ablation.
• The goal is R0 resection while strictly preserving hepatic inflow/outflow.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.
2. Address the primary colon tumor if symptomatic or locally advanced : start with laparoscopic assessment to evaluate PCI score and consider en-bloc left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the left colon primary) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with cytoreductive surgery (i.e. excision of all peritoneal nodules) with or without HIPEC according to response and patient condition.
• The sequence (primary first vs liver-first) depends on technical considerations and necessity of HIPEC.

E. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging of both liver and lungs.

F. If disease remains disseminated
• Continue systemic second-line chemotherapy and consider palliative or symptom-oriented strategies according to MDT.

Step 3 – Critical missing information

B. Exact segmental distribution and vascular relationships of liver lesions.
C. Molecular profile to optimize systemic treatment.
D. Status and symptoms related to the primary colon tumor.
E. Evolution of CEA and radiologic response over time.

G. Confirmation of absence of other extrahepatic disease on full staging.

Case_Content:
Woman, 66 years old, T3N1M1 transverse colon cancer, five liver metastases and two pulmonary nodules at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. RAS wild-type, CEA 420 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Bilateral hepato-pulmonary involvement, potentially treatable sequentially.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has bilateral liver involvement (five metastases) and two pulmonary nodules, constituting extra‑hepatic disease (M1b). Current consensus and the provided literature state that definite pulmonary metastases mandate systemic therapy first and require thoracic MDT input before any curative‑intent surgery. Therefore a prerequisite action – neoadjuvant systemic chemotherapy with response assessment and formal thoracic surgical evaluation of the lung lesions – must be completed before liver (or combined) resection can be planned.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
• Initiate systemic chemotherapy immediately (e.g., 6 cycles of FOLFOX ± bevacizumab or FOLFIRI ± cetuximab, given RAS wild‑type).  
• Restage after chemotherapy with high‑resolution chest CT, liver MRI, and volumetric CT to (a) assess tumor response, (b) calculate future liver remnant (FLR), and (c) confirm resectability of pulmonary nodules.  
• If liver disease remains technically resectable but FLR is borderline, consider portal vein embolization (PVE) or a two‑stage hepatectomy (e.g., right hepatectomy first, hypertrophy, then left‑sided resection).  
• Adopt a liver‑first (reverse) sequencing: perform hepatic resection once adequate FLR and negative margins can be achieved, preserving at least two contiguous segments with intact inflow/outflow and biliary drainage.  
• After hepatic recovery (4–6 weeks), re‑evaluate pulmonary lesions. If ≤3 nodules, peripheral, and pulmonary function is adequate, proceed to staged pulmonary metastasectomy (wedge resections or segmentectomy) – preferably via minimally invasive thoracoscopy.  
• If pulmonary lesions are not surgically resectable or patient fitness is limited, treat them with stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) or percutaneous ablation (RFA/ microwave).  
• Continue systemic therapy post‑operatively (adjuvant or maintenance) for a total of 6–12 months, adjusting regimen based on response and tolerability.  
• Throughout, maintain multidisciplinary review (colorectal, hepatobiliary, thoracic surgeons, medical oncology, radiology, anesthesia) and reassess at each decision point.

Step 3 - Missing data  
• Quantitative liver function assessment (ICG clearance, Child‑Pugh, MELD) and precise volumetry to determine FLR.  
• Detailed size, segmental location, and relationship to major vessels of each liver metastasis.  
• Exact size, location (lobe, segment), and number of pulmonary nodules; presence of mediastinal/hilar nodes.  
• Pulmonary function tests (FEV1, DLCO) and cardiopulmonary fitness (ECOG/ASA).  
• Patient’s comorbidity profile (cardiovascular, diabetes, renal, etc.) and performance status.  
• Prior treatments (any neoadjuvant therapy already given, prior surgeries).  
• Patient preferences regarding aggressive multimodal therapy versus palliative approach.

The patient presents with five liver metastases and two pulmonary nodules in the setting of a T3N1 transverse colon cancer, without other reported sites. • Perform high-resolution liver MRI and chest CT to confirm exact number, distribution, and resectability of both liver and lung lesions.

• Start systemic chemotherapy (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± anti-EGFR given RAS wild-type status).
• The objective is to assess tumor biology and confirm disease control at hepatic and pulmonary sites.

C. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI, and thoraco-abdominal enhanced CT-scan every 2-3 months to evaluate response and detect any potential reduction in tumor burden that could open a limited local treatment window.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

D. Criteria for secondary resectability
• Surgery can be considered only if chemotherapy induces:
– Significant reduction in lesion size and number in both liver and lung.
– Feasibility of staged or parenchymal-sparing resections with adequate future liver remnant.

E. Potential surgical strategies for liver metastases if response is favorable
• Two-stage hepatectomy or combined parenchymal-sparing resections depending on response pattern.
• Portal vein embolization / venous deprivation / ALPPS may be required if major hepatectomy becomes necessary.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

• Extended right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon primary) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) should be coordinated according to response and patient condition (ideally after liver surgery).
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for colectomy.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

G. Management of the lung metastases
• Plan pulmonary metastasectomy or ablative treatment in a staged manner.
• Preoperative evaluation of respiratory function

• Continue second-line systemic therapy or adapt regimen (such as intra-arterial chemotherapy after resection of the primary tumor) according to MDT, with possible consideration of local ablative techniques.
• Continue systemic third-line chemotherapy and consider palliative or symptom-oriented strategies according to MDT.

• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging of both liver and lungs.

Response:

Not resectable

Mediastinal nodes generally require thoracic surgery and are considered distant metastases; their presence together with a very high CEA (680 ng/mL) and KRAS mutation suggests aggressive biology. Consequently, an R0 resection of all disease cannot be achieved at this time, making the case unresectable.

   – Consider portal vein embolization if future liver remnant would be <30 % after planned hepatectomy.

• Offer enrollment in a clinical trial exploring novel conversion strategies or immunotherapy if microsatellite status is assessed and appropriate.

Case_Content:
Woman, 60 years old, T4N2 rectal tumor, six bilobar liver metastases, pulmonary micronodules at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan, CEA 1250 ng/mL, RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Extensive hepato-pulmonary involvement, not resectable upfront.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has six bilobar liver metastases and pulmonary micronodules, which currently preclude an R0 resection. However, conversion to resectability is possible if (a) systemic chemotherapy achieves sufficient tumor shrinkage and disease control in both liver and lung, and (b) the pulmonary lesions are proven to be limited and amenable to curative local therapy (wedge resection, segmentectomy, or SBRT). These two prerequisites are explicit actions that must be completed before a definitive surgical plan can be made.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
• Initiate intensive systemic therapy: 6‑8 cycles of a triplet regimen (FOLFOXIRI) combined with anti‑EGFR antibody (cetuximab) because the tumor is RAS wild‑type and the disease burden is high.  
• Concurrently deliver short‑course radiotherapy (5 × 5 Gy) to the rectal primary, followed by a rest period to allow tumor down‑staging.  
• Re‑stage with high‑resolution liver MRI and thin‑slice chest CT after 2–3 months of chemotherapy: assess response of liver lesions (size, number, distribution) and characterize pulmonary nodules (size ≤10 mm, number ≤3, location amenable to wedge resection or SBRT).  
• If liver disease shows ≥30 % future liver remnant (FLR) after planned resection, proceed to conversion surgery; if FLR would be <30 %, schedule portal vein embolization (PVE) or consider associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to induce hypertrophy.  
• Surgical sequence (liver‑first approach):  
   – Stage 1: Perform right portal vein embolization (or ALPPS first stage) to hypertrophy left liver.  
   – Stage 2 (≈4–6 weeks later): Execute curative‑intent liver resection (e.g., right hepatectomy with non‑anatomic left‑lateral resections or a two‑stage hepatectomy) aiming for R0 margins while preserving ≥2 contiguous segments.  
   – Simultaneously or shortly thereafter, address pulmonary metastases: perform video‑assisted thoracoscopic wedge resections of all resectable nodules, or deliver SBRT if resection would compromise pulmonary reserve.  
• After hepatic and pulmonary clearance, proceed to definitive rectal surgery (low anterior resection with total mesorectal excision or abdominoperineal resection, depending on sphincter involvement) after confirming adequate recovery and oncologic response.  
• Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy (additional 4–6 cycles of FOLFOX or CAPOX) to consolidate systemic control.  
• Throughout, maintain multidisciplinary monitoring (HPB surgeon, thoracic surgeon, colorectal surgeon, medical oncologist, radiation oncologist, radiologist, anesthesiologist) and assess functional reserve (liver function tests, indocyanine‑green clearance, pulmonary function tests) before each operative step.

Step 3 - Missing data  
• Exact size and anatomical location of each liver metastasis; volumetric calculation of future liver remnant.  
• Number, size, and precise distribution of pulmonary nodules; pulmonary function test results (FEV1, DLCO).  
• Patient’s performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidities (cardiovascular, renal, hepatic).  
• Baseline laboratory values (bilirubin, albumin, INR, liver enzymes).  
• Details of rectal tumor involvement (distance from anal verge, invasion of adjacent organs, response to any neoadjuvant radiotherapy).  
• Prior systemic therapy received (agents, cycles, response assessment).  
• Imaging modality used for staging (contrast‑enhanced CT vs. MRI) and quality of radiologic assessment.  
• Patient’s preferences regarding aggressive multimodality treatment versus palliation.

The patient presents with six bilobar liver metastases and pulmonary micronodules in the context of a T4N2 rectal tumor and very high CEA (1250 ng/mL). The combination of extensive bilobar hepatic disease and extrahepatic pulmonary involvement reflects advanced systemic dissemination. From a hepatobiliary perspective, this situation is considered unresectable upfront.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Comprehensive staging and multidisciplinary planning
• Perform high-resolution liver and pelvic MRI and chest CT to confirm exact number, distribution, and resectability of both liver and lung lesions.
• Thoracic surgical assessment of pulmonary nodules is required.

• The objective is to assess tumor biology and confirm disease control at hepatic and pulmonary sites.

• Perform high-resolution liver MRI, and thoraco-abdominal enhanced CT-scan every 2-3 months to evaluate response and detect any potential reduction in tumor burden that could open a limited local treatment window.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

D. Criteria for secondary resectability
• Surgery can be considered only if chemotherapy induces:
– Significant reduction in lesion size and number in both liver and lung.
– Feasibility of staged or parenchymal-sparing resections with adequate future liver remnant.

E. Potential surgical strategies for liver metastases if response is favorable
• Hepatobiliary surgical re-evaluation would be considered only in the rare case of major response with significant reduction of both hepatic and pulmonary disease, allowing complete clearance of all sites.
• Two-stage hepatectomy or combined parenchymal-sparing resections depending on response pattern.
• Portal vein embolization / venous deprivation / ALPPS may be required if major hepatectomy becomes necessary.

Case_Content:
Man, 58 years old, left colon cancer, liver metastases (segments IV, V, VIII) and confirmed right iliac bone metastasis at the abdominal CT scan. KRAS mutated.
MDT Discussion: Hepato-osseous involvement, priority systemic management.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has liver metastases in segments IV, V and VIII that are technically resectable, but there is a confirmed right iliac bone metastasis representing extra‑hepatic disease. Current guidelines consider limited extra‑hepatic disease (oligometastatic) potentially resectable only after systemic therapy has demonstrated disease control and after the extra‑hepatic site has been addressed (e.g., radiotherapy, SBRT, or surgical stabilization). Therefore a prerequisite action – systemic chemotherapy (and possibly local treatment of the bone lesion) – must be completed before a definitive liver (and colon) resection can be planned.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
• Initiate systemic chemotherapy immediately: preferred regimen FOLFOX + bevacizumab (KRAS‑mutated disease excludes anti‑EGFR agents); consider intensification to FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab if patient fitness allows.  
• Re‑evaluate after 2–3 months with triphasic CT or MRI of the liver, PET‑CT for extra‑hepatic disease, and bone scan/MRI of the iliac lesion. Document response (RECIST) and assess CEA trend.  
• If liver lesions have responded (≥30 % shrinkage) and no new lesions appear, proceed to local management of the bone metastasis:  
 – For a solitary, non‑painful iliac lesion, stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) is preferred;  
 – If structural compromise or pain exists, consider surgical fixation or curettage followed by radiotherapy.  
• Re‑assess future liver remnant (FLR) volume using volumetric CT. If projected FLR < 30 % (or < 40 % after chemotherapy), schedule portal vein embolization (PVE) of the right portal branches to hypertrophy the left lateral segments (II‑III).  
• After adequate hypertrophy (typically 4–6 weeks post‑PVE) and confirmed disease control, plan definitive surgery:  
 – Option A (simultaneous): right trisectionectomy (segments IV‑VIII) combined with left‑sided hemicolectomy in a single operation if operative risk acceptable (patient ASA I‑II, good cardiopulmonary reserve).  
 – Option B (staged): first perform the major hepatectomy (right trisectionectomy) after PVE, then, after 4–6 weeks of recovery, perform left hemicolectomy. Staging reduces operative time and allows better postoperative monitoring.  
• Aim for R0 resection of all liver lesions with a ≥10 mm margin when feasible; use intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm margins.  
• Post‑operative adjuvant systemic therapy (same regimen or switch to second‑line if progression) for at least 6 months, with consideration of maintenance bevacizumab.  
• Ongoing surveillance: CT/MRI of liver every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months; bone imaging as indicated.

Step 3 - Missing data  
• Performance status (ECOG/WHO) and detailed comorbidity profile (cardiopulmonary reserve, ASA class).  
• Baseline liver function tests and indocyanine‑green clearance or similar assessment of hepatic reserve.  
• Precise size and number of each liver metastasis; volumetric measurement of total tumor burden.  
• Quantitative FLR calculation (percentage of total liver volume).  
• Detailed characteristics of the iliac bone lesion (size, cortical involvement, pain, pathological fracture risk).  
• Baseline tumor markers (CEA, CA 19‑9, LDH).  
• Full staging PET‑CT to exclude additional occult extra‑hepatic disease.  
• Patient preference regarding surgical sequencing and willingness for intensive systemic therapy.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with liver metastases in segments IV, V, and VIII associated with a confirmed right iliac bone metastasis in the context of a left colon cancer. The presence of osseous metastatic disease indicates systemic dissemination beyond the liver and excludes any curative hepatobiliary surgical strategy. From a hepatobiliary perspective, this situation is considered unresectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Systemic therapy as primary strategy (mandatory)
• Initiate or adapt systemic chemotherapy according to MDT decision (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab; KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR).
•Perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Management of bone metastasis
• Integrate radiotherapy and/or orthopedic evaluation for the right iliac lesion depending on symptoms and fracture risk.

C. Radiologic reassessment
• Perform periodic liver MRI and whole-body imaging to monitor response.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

D. Role of liver-directed therapy
• Liver surgery is not indicated unless an exceptional systemic response with control of bone disease occurs, which remains unlikely.

E. If insufficient response and if disease remains disseminated
• Continue second-line systemic therapy according to MDT, and consider palliative or symptom-oriented strategies according to MDT.

B. Extent and symptoms related to the iliac bone metastasis.
C. chest CT scan
perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT
dosage CEA level 
D. Molecular profile beyond KRAS status to optimize treatment.
E. Status and symptoms related to the primary colon tumor.
F. Evolution of CEA and radiologic response over time.

Case_Content:
Woman, 69 years old, T3N1 rectal tumor with two liver metastases and an isolated left pulmonary nodule at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. RAS wild-type, CEA 210 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Limited hepato-pulmonary involvement, possibility of a combined approach depending on response.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has a resectable‑appearing primary (T3N1 rectal cancer) and only two liver metastases, but critical technical details are absent: exact size and segmental location of the hepatic lesions, estimated future liver remnant (FLR) after resection, and the anatomic characteristics of the left pulmonary nodule (size, proximity to hilar structures, pulmonary reserve). These pieces of information are decisive for determining whether an R0 hepatic resection can be achieved while preserving ≥2 contiguous liver segments with adequate inflow/outflow and whether the lung lesion can be safely removed (wedge vs segmentectomy) or observed. Because these data are missing, surgery cannot be performed upfront; however, they are obtainable, so the case is classified as “Potentially resectable”.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initial staging and functional assessment  
  • Obtain high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast and a dedicated thoracic CT (or PET‑CT) to define lesion size, number, and relationship to vascular/biliary structures.  
  • Perform pulmonary function tests and cardiopulmonary evaluation to confirm fitness for thoracic surgery.  
  • Calculate FLR using volumetric software; if FLR <30 % (or <0.5 %/kg), plan portal vein embolization (PVE) or consider a two‑stage hepatectomy.  

- Neoadjuvant therapy  
  • Because the primary is rectal, give short‑course pelvic radiotherapy (5 × 5 Gy) or long‑course chemoradiation depending on sphincter preservation goals.  
  • Start systemic chemotherapy for metastatic disease: preferred regimen is FOLFOX (or CAPOX) combined with anti‑EGFR antibody (cetuximab) given RAS wild‑type, or with bevacizumab if anti‑EGFR not feasible. Aim for 3–4 cycles, then restage.  

- Response assessment  
  • Re‑image liver and lung after chemotherapy (RECIST 1.1 and morphologic criteria).  
  • If hepatic lesions have responded sufficiently to allow an R0 resection with adequate FLR, and the pulmonary nodule remains ≤10 mm, stable, and resectable, proceed to surgery.  

- Surgical sequencing (individualized)  
  1. Liver‑first approach (preferred when hepatic disease dominates):  
     – Perform hepatic resection (anatomical or non‑anatomical) preserving ≥2 contiguous segments; use intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm clearance.  
     – If FLR was borderline, combine with pre‑operative PVE or ALPPS as needed.  
     – Within 4–6 weeks, perform thoracoscopic wedge resection of the left lung nodule (or segmentectomy if larger).  
     – Finally, after recovery (6–8 weeks), complete low anterior resection of the rectum with a protective loop ileostomy, followed by ileostomy reversal later.  

  2. Simultaneous approach (if liver resection is limited, e.g., two peripheral lesions in left lateral segment) and patient has low operative risk:  
     – Combined laparoscopic liver metastasectomy + low anterior resection in the same operation, followed by staged thoracic resection after 4–6 weeks.  

  3. Classic (colon‑first) approach only if rectal symptoms dictate urgent primary control; otherwise, avoid because it risks progression of liver disease.  

- Adjuvant therapy  
  • Resume systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 4–6 additional cycles) after recovery from all resections, tailored to pathologic response and margin status.  
  • Consider postoperative radiotherapy to the pelvis if margin‑positive or high‑risk features persist.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Exact size (maximum diameter) and segmental location of each liver metastasis.  
- Volumetric assessment of future liver remnant (FLR) after planned resection.  
- Presence of additional occult hepatic lesions (intra‑operative ultrasound may reveal).  
- Size, exact location (segment/lobe), and relationship to pulmonary vessels/bronchi of the left lung nodule.  
- Pulmonary function test results and overall performance status (ASA grade).  
- Details of any prior systemic therapy already given (number of cycles, response).  
- Patient’s comorbidities and cardiopulmonary risk assessment.  

These data are essential to move from “potentially resectable” to a definitive surgical plan.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with two liver metastases and a single left pulmonary nodule in the setting of a T3N1 rectal tumor, without other reported sites. Limited, potentially resectable extrahepatic disease (lung) does not preclude a curative-intent strategy if all sites can be completely treated. From a hepatobiliary perspective, the liver disease appears technically amenable to parenchymal-sparing resection with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant. This situation is considered potentially resectable within a multimodal, sequential curative strategy.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Comprehensive staging and multidisciplinary planning
• Perform high-resolution liver and pelvic MRI and chest CT to confirm exact number, distribution, and resectability of both liver and lung lesions.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).
• Thoracic surgical assessment of the lung metastasis is required.
• Pelvic MRI to integrate rectal treatment planning.
• Given the high CEA level (210 ng/mL) and multifocal metastases, perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Initial systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Start systemic doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± anti-EGFR given RAS wild-type status).
• The objective is to assess tumor biology and confirm disease control at hepatic and pulmonary sites.

C. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver and pelvic MRI, and thoraco-abdominal enhanced CT-scan every 2-3 months to evaluate response and detect any potential reduction in tumor burden that could open a limited local treatment window.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

D. Criteria for secondary resectability
• Surgery can be considered only if chemotherapy induces:
– Significant reduction in lesion size and number in both liver and lung.
– Feasibility of staged or parenchymal-sparing resections with adequate future liver remnant.

E. Potential surgical strategies for liver metastases if response is favorable
• Parenchymal-sparing resections or ablation depending on response pattern.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

F. Management of the rectal primary
• Local pelvic treatment (radiotherapy with chemotherapy ± surgery) should be coordinated during the systemic therapy period according to rectal oncologic principles (PRODIGE 23 protocol).
• After restaging with high-resolution pelvic MRI,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : follow up of primary tumor
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : strict follow up of primary tumor
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : rectal resection after appropriate recovery: oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles).
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for rectal resection.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.

G. Management of the single lung metastase
• Plan pulmonary metastasectomy or ablative treatment in a staged manner.
• Preoperative evaluation of respiratory function

I. If insufficient response and if disease remains disseminated
• Continue second-line systemic therapy or adapt regimen according to MDT, with possible consideration of local ablative techniques.

J. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging of both liver and lungs.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution and vascular relationships of the liver metastases.
B. Resectability assessment of the lung lesion by thoracic surgery.
C. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
D. Detailed pelvic MRI to plan rectal treatment.
E. Patient’s performance status for staged multimodal procedures.
F. Confirmation of absence of other extrahepatic disease on full staging.
G. Evolution of CEA and radiologic response over time.
H. Grade of differentiation, MSS/ MSI mutation and molecular status of the primary cancer: influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
I. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Man, 65 years old, right T4N2 colon cancer, eight bilobar liver metastases and moderate peritoneal carcinomatosis at the abdominal CT scan. CEA 970 ng/mL.
MDT Discussion: Extensive hepato-peritoneal disease, goal of systemic control.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Not resectable: The patient has eight bilobar liver metastases and moderate peritoneal carcinomatosis. Even with modern techniques, achieving an R0 resection while preserving at least two contiguous liver segments, adequate inflow/outflow, and a future liver remnant >30 % is highly unlikely. The presence of diffuse peritoneal disease further precludes a curative intent resection of the extra‑hepatic component. Therefore, based on current oncologic and technical criteria, the disease is classified as not resectable at this time.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate intensive systemic chemotherapy as conversion therapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab or a comparable triplet regimen) to attempt tumor down‑staging and assess tumor biology.  
- Obtain baseline molecular profiling (KRAS/NRAS, BRAF, MSI‑H/dMMR) to guide targeted agents and potential immunotherapy.  
- Re‑stage after 2–3 months of therapy with high‑quality contrast‑enhanced MRI (or liver‑specific MRI) and CT of chest/abdomen, plus PET‑CT if available, to evaluate response of liver lesions, peritoneal disease (PCI score), and to calculate future liver remnant volume.  
- Monitor serum CEA serially; a significant decline (e.g., >50 % and trending toward normal) would suggest favorable biology.  
- If imaging shows a marked reduction to ≤4 liver metastases confined to one lobe and peritoneal disease becomes limited (PCI ≤ 3) and resectable, re‑evaluate for a staged surgical approach:  
   • Consider a liver‑first strategy with portal vein embolization (PVE) or two‑stage hepatectomy/ALPPS to secure adequate FLR, followed by resection of the primary colon tumor.  
   • If peritoneal disease remains limited after systemic therapy, discuss cytoreductive surgery plus HIPEC as a combined curative intent.  
- If disease does not respond adequately or progresses, continue systemic therapy, consider enrollment in a clinical trial (e.g., novel targeted or immunotherapy agents), and focus on symptom control and best supportive care.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG/ASA) and comorbidities that affect surgical tolerance.  
- Baseline liver function tests and quantitative future liver remnant (FLR) assessment.  
- Detailed size, exact location, and vascular involvement of each hepatic metastasis.  
- Extent of peritoneal disease quantified by Peritoneal Cancer Index (PCI).  
- Molecular profile of the tumor (KRAS/NRAS, BRAF, MSI‑H/dMMR).  
- Prior or planned neoadjuvant therapy details (if any have already been given).  
- Pulmonary status and any other extra‑hepatic sites (e.g., lung nodules).
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with eight bilobar liver metastases associated with moderate peritoneal carcinomatosis in the context of a right T4N2 colon cancer and markedly elevated CEA (970 ng/mL). The presence of peritoneal dissemination combined with extensive bilobar hepatic disease excludes any curative hepatobiliary surgical approach at this stage. From a hepatobiliary perspective, this situation is considered unresectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Comprehensive staging and multidisciplinary planning
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and enhanced CT to confirm exact number, distribution, and resectability of both liver and peritoneal lesions.
• Given the high CEA level (970 ng/mL) and multifocal metastases, perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Induction systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Administer 2–3 months of peri-operative doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) according to MDT decision to assess tumor biology and optimize oncologic control according to patient tolerance.
• This allows treatment of potential micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology before surgery.

C. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and thoraco-abdominal enhanced CT-scan every 2-3 months to evaluate response and detect any potential reduction in tumor burden that could open a limited local treatment window.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

D. Criteria for reconsidering surgical strategy
• Surgical re-evaluation may be considered only in the rare situation of major response with near-complete control of peritoneal disease and limited residual liver lesions.
• If disease control or response is observed:
	1.	Perform parenchymal-sparing liver resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound : 
• The goal is R0 resection while strictly preserving hepatic inflow/outflow.
2. Address the primary colon tumor if symptomatic or locally advanced : start with laparoscopic assessment to evaluate PCI score and consider en-bloc right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon primary) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with cytoreductive surgery (i.e. excision of all peritoneal nodules) with or without HIPEC according to response and patient condition.
• The sequence (primary first vs liver-first) depends on technical considerations and necessity of HIPEC.

E. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging of both liver and lungs.

F. If disease remains disseminated
• Continue systemic second-line chemotherapy and consider palliative or symptom-oriented strategies according to MDT.

Case_Content:
Man, 59 years old, left T3N1M1 colon tumor, five bilobar liver metastases (1.5-3.5 cm). CEA 1150 ng/mL. KRAS mutated, BRAF wild-type.Liver MRI: contact of segment VIII lesion with middle hepatic vein.
MDT Discussion: Technically resectable disease, high tumor marker suggests systemic risk.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – The liver lesions are technically amenable to resection (five bilobar metastases ≤ 3.5 cm, and the only anatomic issue is contact of the segment VIII lesion with the middle hepatic vein). However, the very high CEA (1150 ng/mL) and KRAS mutation indicate aggressive tumor biology. Current guidelines and the literature cited recommend “proof of time” with neoadjuvant systemic therapy for such biologically high‑risk disease before committing to major liver surgery. Therefore a prerequisite (systemic chemotherapy with response assessment) must be completed before surgery can be safely planned.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Initial systemic therapy (neoadjuvant):  
  • Regimen: FOLFOXIRI (5‑FU, leucovorin, oxaliplatin, irinotecan) + bevacizumab, provided the patient has adequate performance status (ECOG 0‑1) and organ function.  
  • Duration: 6 cycles (≈ 3 months), with restaging MRI/CT after 2–3 months to evaluate tumor response and FLR.  
- Re‑assessment after chemotherapy:  
  • If all lesions have responded or remained stable and no new extra‑hepatic disease appears, proceed to surgical planning.  
  • If a lesion becomes resectable only after downsizing, consider a two‑stage hepatectomy or portal vein embolization (PVE) to augment future liver remnant (target ≥ 30 % of total liver volume).  
  • If the middle hepatic vein involvement persists, plan for segment‑VIII resection with possible venous reconstruction or use of middle hepatic vein‑sparing techniques.  
- Surgical sequence:  
  1. Primary tumor: Left‑sided colon cancer – perform a standard oncologic left hemicolectomy (open or laparoscopic) either before or simultaneously with liver surgery, depending on the extent of hepatic resection.  
  2. Liver resection: Aim for R0 resection of all five metastases, preserving at least two contiguous hepatic segments with adequate inflow/outflow and ≥ 30 % FLR. Options include:  
     – Single‑stage extended right or left hepatectomy with selective segmental resections, or  
     – Two‑stage approach (first clearing lesions in one lobe, PVE, then second‑stage resection of the contralateral lobe).  
- Post‑operative (adjuvant) therapy:  
  • Complete a further 3–6 months of systemic chemotherapy (same backbone, possibly de‑escalated to FOLFOX + bevacizumab) based on pathology (margin status, nodal status) and postoperative recovery.  
- If disease progresses on neoadjuvant therapy:  
  • Re‑evaluate for conversion strategies (e.g., hepatic arterial infusion, Y‑90 radio‑embolisation) or local ablative modalities (RFA/SBRT) for unresectable lesions.  
  • Consider palliative systemic therapy if curative intent is no longer feasible.

Step 3 – Missing data  
- Patient’s performance status (ECOG) and detailed comorbidity profile (Charlson index).  
- Baseline liver function tests and volumetric assessment of future liver remnant.  
- Full extra‑hepatic staging (chest CT/PET, abdominal imaging for peritoneal disease).  
- Extent of vascular involvement: length of contact with the middle hepatic vein and whether encasement or invasion is present.  
- Patient’s preferences regarding staged versus simultaneous resections and willingness for intensive chemotherapy.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with five bilobar liver metastases (1.5–3.5 cm), including a segment VIII lesion in contact with the middle hepatic vein, without reported extrahepatic disease. From a technical standpoint, complete clearance with parenchymal-sparing resections appears feasible while preserving an adequate future liver remnant. According to hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is potentially resectable. However, the very high CEA level (1150 ng/mL) suggests aggressive tumor biology and a high systemic risk.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT to confirm the relationship of the 5 lesions to segment VIII vascular and biliary structures. Precise anatomical mapping is required to plan a safe parenchymal-sparing resection and a chest CT scan
• Given the high CEA level (1150 ng/mL), perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Preoperative systemic therapy
• The elevated CEA level (1150 ng/mL) and multiplicity of lesions suggest biologically active disease.
• Give 3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) to treat potential micrometastatic disease and assess tumor biology.
• KRAS mutation excludes anti-EGFR therapy.
• This period treats micrometastatic disease and evaluates tumor biology.

C. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to confirm maintained resectability and evaluate vascular/biliary relationships.
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).

D. Surgical management (staged strategy)
• If restaging confirms continued resectability, perform a first multiple atypical resection for the 5 lesions and/or segmentectomy 8 with en-bloc partial resection a the middle hepatic veine removing the 5 metastases, or a formal right hepatectomy if anatomically more appropriate, and if volume of the remnant liver is sufficient, aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin .
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for both liver resection and colectomy.
• Preoperative prehabilitation and ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocols are evidence-based, multidisciplinary strategies designed to optimize patient health before surgery and accelerate recovery afterward.
• After recovery, perform left hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the left colon cancer) with lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) with primary anastomosis 

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy (including the pre operative cycles). 
• Monitor CEA and imaging at 3 month intervals given the elevated initial tumor marker (CEA 1150 ng/mL).

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy. 
B. Precise segmental distribution of the three lesions within the left liver and detailed vascular/biliary relationship of the liver lesion – essential to confirm that a non anatomic resection will achieve clear margins without compromising hepatic inflow/outflow.  
C. Radiologic tumor response after systemic chemotherapy (decrease, stability or progression) and evolution of CEA
D. a chest CT scan
E. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Woman, 62 years old, right T4aN2M1 colon cancer, seven liver metastases (2-5 cm) at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 1600 ng/mL. BRAF V600E mutation, MSS.
MDT Discussion: Extensive liver disease, poor prognosis linked to molecular profile.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable  
- Seven hepatic metastases (2‑5 cm) are technically not an absolute barrier; modern criteria allow resection of multiple, bilobar lesions provided an adequate future liver remnant (FLR) can be preserved.  
- The patient’s aggressive biology (BRAF V600E, CEA 1600 ng/mL, synchronous T4a primary) predicts a high risk of early progression; therefore a “proof‑of‑time” approach with neoadjuvant systemic therapy is required before committing to surgery.  
- Key prerequisite actions before surgery: (a) systemic chemotherapy (preferably an intensive regimen with a BRAF‑directed component) to assess tumor responsiveness and (b) quantitative volumetric imaging (CT‑volumetry or MRI) to confirm that an FLR ≥ 30 % (or ≥ 0.5 % body‑weight) can be left, with portal vein embolisation (PVE) or a staged hepatectomy planned if the FLR is insufficient.  

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  
- Induction systemic therapy (4–6 cycles)  
  • Preferred regimen: FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab combined with a BRAF‑targeted triplet (e.g., encorafenib + cetuximab ± binimetinib) per current BRAF‑mutant mCRC protocols.  
  • Goal: achieve tumor shrinkage, assess disease biology (response vs. progression), and allow time for FLR hypertrophy if PVE is performed.

  • CEA every 3 months, cross‑sectional imaging (CT or MRI) every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.

Case_Content:
Man, 66 years old, T3N2 upper rectal cancer with four liver metastases at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 980 ng/mL, RAS wild-type, MSI-H.
MDT Discussion: Bilobar metastases with MSI-H profile opening discussion for first-line immunotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment  
Category: Potentially resectable  

Reasoning: The patient has four bilobar liver metastases, but no information is provided on the individual lesion size, exact segmental distribution, volumetric liver data (future liver remnant % or FLR g/kg), baseline liver function, or performance status. These parameters are decisive for determining whether an R0 resection can be achieved while preserving adequate hepatic reserve. Because these data are missing, the case cannot be classified as “Resectable upfront.” At the same time, there is no absolute contraindication (e.g., unresectable extra‑hepatic disease, invasion of major vascular structures) that would render the disease “Not resectable.” Therefore, the case is deemed potentially resectable pending further assessment and/or down‑staging.

Step 2 – Oncological strategy  

1. Induction systemic therapy – Initiate first‑line immune checkpoint inhibition appropriate for MSI‑H metastatic colorectal cancer (e.g., pembrolizumab 200 mg q3 weeks or nivolumab + ipilimumab per current ESMO/ASCO guidelines).  
2. Concurrent rectal management –  
    If the rectal tumor is symptomatic (bleeding, obstruction) or threatens the mesorectal fascia, give short‑course radiotherapy (5 × 5 Gy) followed by a waiting interval of 4–6 weeks.  
    If asymptomatic, radiotherapy can be deferred until after hepatic disease control, using the interval to assess response to immunotherapy.  
3. Restaging (after 2–3 months of immunotherapy) – Perform high‑resolution liver MRI with hepatobiliary contrast and repeat thoraco‑abdominal CT. Assess:  
    Change in size/number of liver lesions (RECIST).  
    FLR volume using volumetric software.  
    Any new extra‑hepatic sites.  
4. Decision point –  
    If liver disease is now technically resectable (all lesions amenable to R0 resection with FLR ≥ 30 % or ≥ 0.5 % body‑weight) proceed to hepatic surgery.  
    If FLR is insufficient but lesions are otherwise resectable, plan portal vein embolization (PVE) or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) to induce hypertrophy, then re‑operate after 4–6 weeks.  
    If disease remains extensive (>70 % liver volume required, progression, or new extra‑hepatic sites), continue systemic therapy (consider adding a targeted agent if RAS‑wild‑type and disease biology warrants) and reassess later.  
5. Hepatic surgery – Prefer a liver‑first (or “reverse”) approach:  
    Perform a staged or single‑stage hepatectomy based on lesion distribution and FLR.  
    Use intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion clearance; aim for R0 margins (≥1 mm).  
    Consider adjunctive thermal ablation for lesions in difficult locations if needed to preserve parenchyma.  
6. Rectal primary – After hepatic resection and recovery (≈6–8 weeks), complete definitive treatment of the rectal cancer:  
    If long‑course chemoradiotherapy was given, proceed with low anterior resection (LAR) or abdominoperineal resection depending on sphincter involvement.  
    If only short‑course RT was used, perform LAR with a protective diverting loop ileostomy; reverse ileostomy after healing.  
7. Adjuvant therapy – Post‑operative systemic therapy may be continued (maintenance immunotherapy or combination with fluoropyrimidine/oxaliplatin) based on pathology (margin status, nodal involvement) and multidisciplinary consensus.  
8. Surveillance – Follow‑up with CEA, 6‑monthly CT/MRI of chest/abdomen, and colonoscopic evaluation per standard guidelines.

Step 3 – Missing data  

 Exact size (maximum diameter) and segmental location of each of the four liver metastases.  
 Volumetric liver assessment – future liver remnant percentage or absolute volume.  
 Baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count) and indocyanine‑green clearance if available.  
 Patient performance status (ECOG/ASA) and comorbidity burden (Charlson index).  
 Detailed pelvic MRI of the rectal tumor – mesorectal fascia involvement, distance to sphincter, presence of threatened adjacent organs.  
 Presence or absence of extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum, distant nodes) on staging CT/PET.  
 Current symptoms from the rectal primary (bleeding, obstruction, pain).  
 Baseline nutritional status and weight.  

These data are essential to confirm technical resectability, to plan the extent of hepatic resection or need for hypertrophy procedures, and to decide the optimal sequencing of rectal and liver surgery.

MDT Discussion: Limited involvement but HER2 mutation may influence systemic therapeutic strategy.

Potentially resectable – the two metastases are confined to segments II and III, which are technically amenable to a left‑lateral sectionectomy. However, definitive surgical feasibility depends on (a) quantitative assessment of the future liver remnant (FLR) volume, (b) the patient’s performance status and comorbidity burden, and (c) confirmation that there is no occult extra‑hepatic disease. These pieces of information are currently missing, so resection cannot be declared upfront.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Complete staging work‑up  
  • Multiphasic liver MRI (or contrast‑enhanced CT) with volumetric analysis to calculate FLR.  
  • Chest CT or PET‑CT to exclude pulmonary or other extra‑hepatic metastases.  
  • Full laboratory panel: liver function tests, bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count.  
  • Assessment of ECOG performance status and Charlson comorbidity index.  
- Molecular‑directed systemic therapy  
  • HER2 positivity warrants incorporation of HER2‑targeted agents (e.g., trastuzumab + pertuzumab) combined with a doublet chemotherapy backbone (FOLFOX or CAPOX).  
  • KRAS/NRAS and MSI status should be confirmed; if KRAS/NRAS wild‑type and MSI‑stable, anti‑EGFR therapy is not indicated because HER2‑directed therapy is preferred.  
- Neoadjuvant phase (if FLR borderline or to test tumor biology)  
  • 2–3 months of HER2‑targeted doublet chemotherapy.  
  • Restaging MRI to evaluate response and re‑measure FLR.  
- Surgical plan (once resectability confirmed)  
  • If the patient is fit (ECOG 0‑1, adequate FLR ≥ 30 % of total liver volume), perform simultaneous curative resection: left‑sided colectomy (segmental or hemicolectomy) plus left‑lateral sectionectomy (segments II‑III).  
  • If simultaneous surgery is deemed unsafe (e.g., marginal FLR, significant comorbidity), adopt a staged approach: resect the primary tumor first, allow recovery, then proceed to liver resection after reassessment.  
- Adjuvant therapy  
  • Continue HER2‑directed therapy together with standard adjuvant chemotherapy (e.g., 6 months of FOLFOX + trastuzumab/pertuzumab) post‑operatively, provided postoperative recovery is uncomplicated.  
- Follow‑up  
  • Serial CEA monitoring (baseline 320 ng/mL) and imaging (CT/MRI) every 3–4 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months up to 5 years.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- ECOG performance status and detailed comorbidity profile (Charlson index).  
- Quantitative liver function and volumetry (future liver remnant percentage).  
- Confirmation of absence of extra‑hepatic disease (chest imaging, PET‑CT).  
- KRAS/NRAS mutation status and microsatellite instability / dMMR status.  
- Detailed anatomic description of the primary colon tumor’s relationship to surrounding structures (to confirm feasibility of simultaneous resection).  
- Baseline hepatic laboratory values (bilirubin, AST/ALT, INR, albumin, platelets).  
- Nutritional assessment (weight loss, albumin, BMI).

Man, 55 years old, right T4N2M1 colon cancer, nine bilobar metastases at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 2500 ng/mL, KRAS mutated.Liver  MRI: infiltration of the right portal pedicle.
MDT Discussion: Major liver involvement, vascular invasion compromising resectability.
Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
Reasoning: The patient has nine bilobar liver metastases with infiltration of the right portal pedicle, which makes an R0 resection impossible with the current liver volume and vascular anatomy. Conversion to resectability will require (a) systemic chemotherapy to downsize the lesions and assess tumor biology, and (b) a hypertrophy‑inducing maneuver (portal vein embolisation or a two‑stage hepatectomy) to obtain an adequate future liver remnant. These prerequisite actions are clearly defined, therefore the case fits the “Potentially resectable” category.

- Initiate intensive conversion chemotherapy: FOLFOXIRI + bevacizumab (KRAS‑mutated disease, high tumour burden).  
- Re‑stage with contrast‑enhanced MRI/CT after 2–3 months to evaluate response, number of viable lesions, and FLR volume.  
- If ≥ 30 % FLR is projected after right‑sided resection, proceed to portal vein embolisation of the left portal branches to induce hypertrophy (target FLR ≥ 40 %).  
- Plan a staged hepatic approach:  
   • Stage 1 – resect or ablate left‑lobe lesions (or perform left lateral resection) and perform PVE.  
   • Interval of 4–6 weeks for hypertrophy; repeat volumetry.  
   • Stage 2 – extended right hepatectomy with portal vein reconstruction (if tumour still involves the right portal pedicle) aiming for R0 margins; intra‑operative ultrasound to locate any residual disease.

- Post‑operative adjuvant chemotherapy (same regimen) for at least 6 months, adjusted to response and tolerance.  
- If chemotherapy fails to achieve sufficient down‑staging or FLR remains inadequate, consider alternative locoregional therapies (radiofrequency ablation, stereotactic body radiotherapy) for residual lesions, or shift to palliative systemic therapy.

- Baseline liver function tests and indocyanine‑green clearance to assess hepatic reserve.  
- Quantitative future liver remnant volume calculation before any intervention.  
- Detailed description of the extent of right portal pedicle invasion (length of involvement, feasibility of vascular reconstruction).  
- Confirmation of absence or presence of extra‑hepatic disease (lung, peritoneum) on PET‑CT or high‑resolution thoracic CT.  
- Baseline CEA trend and other tumour markers after initial chemotherapy cycles.  
- Patient’s preference regarding aggressive surgical strategies versus palliative approach.

1. Induction systemic therapy  
   - Start 6 cycles of intensive chemotherapy (FOLFOXIRI) combined with bevacizumab (RAS‑mutated disease).

Response:
Step 1 - Potentially resectable  
- The segment VII metastasis invades the inferior vena cava (IVC) over a length of >1 cm, a situation that generally requires complex vascular reconstruction and careful assessment of oncologic benefit.  
- No information is provided on the future liver remnant (FLR) volume or on the patient’s hepatic functional reserve, which are decisive for any major hepatectomy.  
- Because the FLR assessment is missing and because down‑staging systemic therapy may be needed to reduce tumor burden and improve the chance of an R0 resection with safe margins, the case cannot be classified as “Resectable upfront.” The prerequisite of a quantified FLR (≥30 % of total liver volume or ≥0.5 % body‑weight) must be obtained before a definitive surgical plan can be made.  

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate intensive neoadjuvant systemic therapy: FOLFOXIRI (5‑FU, oxaliplatin, irinotecan) combined with anti‑EGFR monoclonal antibody (cetuximab) given the RAS‑wild‑type status, aiming for maximal tumor shrinkage and biologic response assessment.  
- Re‑image the liver (contrast‑enhanced MRI or CT) after 2–3 cycles (≈6 weeks) to evaluate:  
   • Change in size/number of all metastases, especially the IVC‑invading lesion.  
   • Residual IVC involvement (partial vs. circumferential).  
   • Calculate FLR volume using volumetric software.
